subtopic: STEPS TO RELIEVE PRESSURE ON U.K. RESERVES
speechtext:
I wish to confirm the statement issued in London today indicating that the Bank of Canada in conjunction with the central banks of ten other countries and the Bank for International Settlements is co-operating in the establishment of a system of currency swap facilities with the Bank of England. The object of these facilities is to relieve pressure on the official reserves of the United Kingdom that may arise from fluctuations in the sterling balances of overseas countries. The participation of the Bank of Canada has been fully discussed with the government.
In the interests of the most effective operation of the measures it is not proposed to go into any detail beyond that released by the Bank of England. The new arrangement will come into effect on June 15, when the facilities made available last September expire.

maintopic: TABLING OF VOLUME 1 OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON CHEMICALS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TABLING OF VOLUME 1 OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON CHEMICALS
speechtext:
I am tabling today copies in English and in French of volume 1 of the Tariff Board's report on reference 120, chemicals. I am tabling also a transcript of the evidence presented at the public hearings of the board.
The report came from the Queen's Printer only this morning. I know there is widespread interest in its contents, and for this reason I have tabled it without delay. It had been hoped to have the report available for sale at the government book shops outside of Ottawa on the date of tabling. However, because of the time factor, this has not proven possible.
This review of the chemical industry is the most extensive study which has ever been undertaken by the board. Recognizing the importance of this report for the Kennedy round of tariff negotiations in Geneva, the board has departed from its usual custom of submitting at one time a complete report. Volume 1 of the report contains only the schedule of tariff items recommended by the Tariff Board, a short prefatory note and certain statistical information. The summary and conclusions, notes on existing and recommended items and general information on the industry will be sent to me in subsequent volumes which I will make public as quickly as possible.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I have not yet had an opportunity to study the recommendations in the board's report. I can, however, assure hon. members that the government will give full consideration to these recommendations.
In this connection I would urge interested parties who may wish to comment on this report to do so promptly. Representations should initially be made in writing and addressed to the director, tariffs division, Department of Finance, Ottawa. A technical group of tariff specialists will be set up shortly to hear oral representations.

I wish to report to the house on developments over the week end in connection with the longshoremen's strike.
A small committee of the cabinet met with the bargaining committees of the I.L.A. and the shipping federation here in Ottawa in continuous session all day Saturday and Sunday morning. In these intensive mediation efforts, my colleagues and I were assisted by Judge Rene Lippe and senior officials of the Department of Labour.
While these sessions did not result in agreement on all the issues in dispute, substantial progress-what I would describe as real progress-was made in further reducing the matters in dispute, so much so that the

I.L.A. union in Trois-Rivieres this morning wired me its acceptance of the final proposals, subject only to clarification of some points with the employers.
The desire for an early settlement of this dispute, which was clearly in evidence over the week end, was further emphasized by a request from the I.L.A. to the Prime Minister this morning for a further meeting, conveyed by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress. Arrangements have been made to bring small ad hoc committees of both parties to Ottawa, distinct from the larger ones we have had here over the week end, for further meetings this afternoon. The urgent request received by the Prime Minister from the

There are no other adjectives I can use to describe it. It has been a showcase of complete dilatoriness on a matter affecting all Canada; and they laugh and sneer. They find it funny. In every part of this nation people should know their reactions. Today we are treated to another of these explanations and postponements. While this has been going on, trade is diminishing. Warnings have been given by the wheat board as to the potential loss which may be suffered. Goods are piling up, and the government says "Wait for a longer while."
One has only to look at the picture in the Gazette this morning to realize that it was not a very happy conclusion. Never before have there been three standing together looking so disheartened and dismayed. The only one who really stood out was the Minister of Transport. That face of his could not have done any harm. Indeed, he stood out as the one who at least had not lost hope. The other two were disheartened, dishevelled and disappointed. Why wasn't the minister of manpower there? He is the only one who knows

anything about labour problems. I say to the Prime Minister with great respect-

subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Sure; I know with great respect.

subtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
-that while these people met together and talked, he travelled. Important as are outside responsibilities, there was no reason why, on an occasion such as this he, the Prime Minister, having regard to Canada's serious economic crisis, should not have been here to do his part. This afternoon the paper reports that he is now going to step in. Why did he not do so during the weeks and weeks that have passed?
The explanation given by the minister is inadequate and meaningless. We have had it over and over again. Last Thursday the Prime Minister expressed the hope that a settlement was anticipated. It is no wonder that the press of the nation has been so critical, and, epitomizing that criticism, this morning's Gazette says "Pitiful Inaction in Ottawa." There is no better description of a government that does not know what to do and is doing its best to prove that it does not. The delay has gone on, and on, and on.
As I said a moment ago, the explanation that is given is entirely inadequate. When the opportunity comes I intend to move the adjournment of the house so we can get to the facts once and for all. On June 1 the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked for leave to move the adjournment of the house. We had a discussion that afternoon. Read it in Hansard. There was the same repetitive explanation by the government. While Canada suffers, her international image is being defaced by the failure of the government to act. All we get is another postponement; wait until this afternoon, or tomorrow, or next week, or some time in the hope that ultimately something may be done.
Parliament should be acting on this. Parliament is ready to act on this. All it requires is a government; but up to the present time the government has shown itself to be a rock of jelly on this problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party welcome the encouraging statement which has been given to the house by the Minister of Labour, and we are glad the negotiations are being resumed this afternoon at four o'clock. We certainly hope those negotiations will result in a settlement of the longshoremen's
June 13, 1966

strike in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec city.
We have hoped all along that a settlement could be reached by the process of collective bargaining. Members of this party are adamantly opposed to compulsory arbitration. However, at the same time we recognize that this strike cannot continue without serious repercussions not only for the economy in general but also for the two parties engaged in the dispute.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
That is why we have suggested some parliamentary intervention which would not result in the imposition of compulsory arbitration, but which would put the workers back on the job with the adoption of those wage increases that have generally been agreed upon, leaving the important point of dispute, namely the reduction in size of work gangs, for continued negotiation with the help of a commissioner of inquiry.
If there is some hope of an immediate settlement then certainly my colleague the hon. member for Skeena will be prepared to allow his bill to stand. I hope that by tomorrow the minister will be able to inform the house and the country that the strike is at an end and that traffic will once more be resumed. I urge upon the minister and the government, however, that if there cannot be a settlement within the next 24 or 48 hours they will not allow the Shipping Federation of Canada to attempt to starve its workers into submission by accepting a 15 per cent reduction in their manpower, which will mean the throwing of older men on the job out on the scrap heap. The federation should not be allowed to do that.
If no settlement is reached within the next 24 or 48 hours I hope the government will give serious consideration to introducing some legislation, not to provide for compulsory arbitration but legislation which will settle the strike on the points which have now been agreed upon, leaving the balance for continued negotiation under the process of free collective bargaining.

Expo on May 31 last, we were told then that if the strike went on great damage would be caused to Expo. That was on May 31 last; it is now June 13 and the strike has not yet been settled.

We are told that a committee made up of a number of ministers was instituted to help solve the strike. Well, there is one minister, namely the minister of manpower (Mr. Marchand), who is a man with experience in industrial relations and who had occasions to settle strikes. In view of the fact that the problem is important, I wonder if he could not make a special effort, a heroic effort to settle that strike. When there was a strike the minister of manpower always said: It must be settled. Now that he is a member of the cabinet, he should do his share to settle that conflict which affects the country's economy and, in particular, the economy of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, we are hearing very optimistic statements but we believe that the government should be realistic and do something to settle that conflict as soon as possible.
If the strike is not over within 24 hours, then the government should take the necessary action to put an end to it as quickly as possible.
Therefore, we hope that the negotiations going on this afternoon will be fruitful, otherwise we will ask the government to take immediately the steps needed to settle the strike within 24 hours at the most.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the calamitous economic paralysis consequent upon the government's failure to bring about an end to the longshoremen's strike in Montreal, Quebec city and Three Rivers, or to take appropriate action toward the resumption of shipping in the face of a critical blockage of grain shipments, disruption of shipping generally, and the serious interference with the timetable of Expo, and the government's continued inactivity with regard to threatened strikes of employees of the St. Lawrence seaway, the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: LACK OF GOVERNMENT ACTION-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Will the hon. member for Ontario kindly address the Chair on the question of urgency of debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: LACK OF GOVERNMENT ACTION-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the urgency of debate is based on the fact that for the past five weeks the nation has been faced with a disruptive strike that affects every aspect of our economy. We have had from day to day, from week to week, assurances by the government that the strike is near the end and that a solution is imminent by the hour. As late as last Thursday the Prime Minister of this country assured this house, and we took his word for it, that the end of the strike was imminent.
Over the week end, according to the press, a 17 hour discussion took place attended by at least three or four ministers, who were not able to bring about a settlement of this strike.

June 13, 1966
Motion for Adjournment Today the Minister of Labour is holding off any action on the part of the government by making another statement that the settlement of the strike is imminent. I do not think this country can stand another delay of 24 hours in view of the disruption of our economy which is affecting every part of this country.
In addition to this strike we are threatened with strikes on the St. Lawrence seaway, the Canadian National Railways and Air Canada, as is set out in my motion. In view of the experience this government has had with the longshoremen's strike, which has already lasted for five weeks, it is surprising that they are still coming up with the same formula of mediation until the last deadline; no doubt we will be faced with strikes which will paralyse this country completely. That is the reason for the urgency which I submit exists in this matter.

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: LACK OF GOVERNMENT ACTION-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there can be no doubt about the importance of the matter which has been introduced by the member for Ontario, and also no doubt about the urgency of finding some very quick solution to the problem he has outlined. It is certain that if the encouraging statement which was made by the minister had not been forthcoming, there would have been every justification for a debate on this matter this afternoon. Hon. members of the opposition are of course in the position of not knowing just how close to a settlement the two disputants are, nor do we know what are the various points still at issue. However, it seems to the members of this party that in view of the statement made by the minister there appears to be a real and genuine hope that the negotiation will be successful, and I fear that a debate at this time might be more injurious than helpful.
I hope the hon. member for Ontario will be prepared to either withdraw his motion or let it stand for 24 hours, and if this matter is not settled by tomorrow and the government has not come up with legislation, then there would be every reason for having the debate. There can be no doubt that the public is impatient and fed up with the long delay in grappling with this problem, but if the longshoremen and the federation are close to a settlement a debate at this time might do more harm than good.
For this reason I hope the hon. member for Ontario will be prepared to postpone his motion until tomorrow in order to give the minister one more chance to try to effect a

satisfactory settlement of this unfortunate dispute.

The question is undisputedly most urgent and pressing. If, at seven o'clock tonight, further to the negotiations which the Minister of Labour and some of his colleagues are to have with the two parties involved, no solution has been found, then I feel we might agree to a resumption of this debate.
If the government does not come up with a solution settlement or does not propose any legislation, then the debate will be necessary so that other members of the cabinet and of the house may suggest motions to settle this strike which has been going on much too long already.
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) said a moment ago, the matter is most urgent. We know that this strike is paralysing many areas of the economy of the country and of the province of Quebec, and we believe it must be settled at the earliest.
If no solution can be found during the discussion which will be held this afternoon, we could then postpone the debate until seven o'clock tonight or, at most, until 2.30 tomorrow afternoon.
Even though we feel the debate is urgent, we would rather await the outcome of the negotiations this afternoon and resume the debate at seven o'clock after private members' hour.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR SUPPLEMENTARY PROVINCIAL ALLOCATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members will recall that the Canada student loans plan came into operation just prior to the beginning of the 1964-65 academic year. This program was the government's first major step in providing student assistance on a large scale toward the objective that all those in Canada who have the scholastic qualifications and who want to get a college education or its vocational equivalent will not be prevented from doing so for financial reasons.
Today, after nearly two years of operation there is no doubt that the Canada student loans plan has been very highly successful in helping to meet this objective. During the first loan year over 42,000 students were assisted under the plan, and in the current loan year up to the end of March loans have been authorized to over 50,000 students, and total loans outstanding under the plan at that time had risen to approximately $57 million.
I would like to recall briefly the main features of the plan and to outline developments in effective demand for student loans during the past two years which give rise to
June 13, 1966

the resolution preceding the measure which will shortly come before the house.
Loans under this plan may be made by banks and certain credit unions to full-time students at universities and other postsecondary educational institutions which have been designated by the participating provinces for purposes of the plan. In keeping with provincial responsibilities in the field of education, the loans are made on the basis of certificates of eligibility which are issued by the participating provinces. A student must obtain a certificate of eligibility before approaching a bank for a loan. A student may qualify for loans up to $1,000 per academic year and up to $5,000 over his entire postsecondary educational career.
The loans made under this legislation are interest and repayment free to the borrowers while they are full-time students, and for the next following six months. During that time interest is paid to the banks and other lenders on behalf of the students by the government of Canada which also guarantees the lenders against loss. After this period, the principal and interest on the loans are repayable by the students on a monthly basis and may be spread over a period of up to ten years from graduation.
The total of loans that may be authorized through the issue of certificates of eligibility, and this is directly relevant to the resolution now before the committee, is limited for each loan year by the total loan provision established by this legislation and by the allocation of this amount among the provinces.
The provincial allocations during the first loan year were determined by dividing the total loan provision of $40 million for that year among all provinces and territories on the basis of population in the 18-24 year age group. Of this amount approximately $27 million was allocated to participating provinces, and approximately $13 million to the province of Quebec which is relying on its own plan and does not participate in the Canada student loans plan. The act provides that this total loan provision will increase each year by the estimated rate of increase of Canada's population in the 18-24 year age group.
The loan provision in the initial legislation was based on the best projection that we, in consultation with provincial officials, could make of the likely demand for student loans. In practice, the demand has exceeded expectations by a considerable margin. The demand for loans even during the first loan
Canada Student Loans Act year pressed against the limits of loan allocations in a few provinces. In November, 1964, the house approved a measure authorizing the Minister of Finance to increase the total allocations of individual provinces during the first loan year up to an aggregate of $8 million.
With the permission of the house, I would like to include in Hansard at this point a table which shows the provincial allocations for the first loan year, and the extent to which they were used.

During the first year of operation, each province administered the plan without much reference to the practices being followed by the other provinces because time had not permitted the development of uniform standards. Careful consideration, however, was given to this subject in a series of federal-provincial meetings of officials during the first year. These consultations resulted in three federal-provincial reports on common administrative criteria for use by the participating provinces during the second loan year.
These reports, which appear in Appendix A to Hansard of June 11, 1965, deal with detailed criteria for determining a student's financial need, his provincial residence status, and certain definitions relating to the designation of educational institutions and other matters.
The process of developing these common criteria has been a continuing one. Improvements and refinements in two of these reports are being worked out, and revised

versions of these reports may soon be agreed to by the provinces and the federal government on the same basis as last year. The development of a co-ordinated approach to the administration of this plan is a fine example of federal-provincial and interprovincial cooperation. It has contributed immeasurably to the successful way in which students have been able to make use of the plan and provides assurance that the plan is being used effectively.
The second loan year began on July 1, 1965. Three months later, at the beginning of the new academic year, it became apparent that loan demand in all provinces was exceeding that experienced during the previous year, and could be expected to exceed by fairly wide margins the provincial allocations for that new loan year.
With the introduction of new agreed criteria governing the authorization of loans, the government was satisfied that this increase reflected a real and effective need for loans by students across Canada.

No. We are proposing by this legislation to enable them to get an additional allocation for this year.
The measure now before the house would, first, increase the total loan provision, or the basic loan provision, for the current loan year from approximately $42 million to $58 million which will be allocated to provinces in the normal way on the basis of population in the 18-24 year age group. The allocations for participating provinces would increase from approximately $28 million to about $39 million. Second, it provides for an additional and discretionary loan provision equal to 20 per cent of the basic loan provision which may be allocated by the minister to provinces as required.
The provision for such a discretionary loan amount recognizes that there have been in practice differences in the levels of relative loan demand from province to province reflecting differences in the number of students, in regional income pattern, in the nature and magnitude of provincial student aid schemes and other factors and that these differences may continue. The existence of these differences makes it desirable not to provide all
6308	COMMONS
Canada Student Loans Act of the needed increase through an across- the-board increase in all provincial allocations, which would result in an unrealistically high over-all loan provision, but to enable the rounding out of individual allocations on a discretionary basis at the request of the province concerned. I would envisage consulting with or informing the other provinces before implementing such a discretionary increase, in view of the close co-operation with provinces on the criteria being applied in the administration of this program.
Escalation of the new, higher basic loan provision from one year to the next would continue on the basis of the growth in the population 18-24 year age group. Similarly, the formula contained in the act for alternative payments to non-participating provinces would remain unaltered. Since this formula is based on payments actually made by the federal government to banks and other lenders in respect of loans made under the legislation, alternative payments will reflect the increase in the volume of lending under the act.
We believe these two changes in the total loan provision to be sufficient to accommodate the loan demand that may arise in any province on the basis of the agreed criteria during the current and subsequent loan years.
The bill contains one other provision which can perhaps be best described as a housekeeping item. The act authorizes the minister to pay interest on loans while the borrowers are full-time students and for a period of six months thereafter, and unintentionally precludes the minister from paying interest on loans in cases where students must for some reason interrupt their education for a period of more than six months, and who later again become full-time students. This is in conflict with the provision which states that loans are interest free to students during any period during which they are full-time students. The proposed amendments will rectify this situation.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this resolution I wish to make it clear that the members of this party will vote in favour of it, but will do so regretfully and indeed under protest because if there is one thing that is obvious about the student loans program it is that it is a far cry from the promises made repeatedly by the present Prime Minister during several election campaigns. This program does what so often is done in Canada: It helps those who need help the least. I am reminded of the old biblical saying, that to him that hath shall be given and from him who hath not shall be taken even that which he hath.
For years this party has proposed that the cost of university education should be carried by the state and that there should be no tuition fee, but that every person who has the ability to go to university should be able to go, regardless of his or his family's ability to pay. When the minister was introducing this resolution he said the same thing, or that the student loans plan was the beginning of that kind of a program. Nothing could be further from the truth; and all the evidence that has been found as a result of studies, and I will refer to some of them later, demonstrate conclusively that we are not, through this loans program or anything else which we have provided, meeting the needs of the children of low income families, whether they live in the cities or in rural areas.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The children of the low income families are not attending university in Canada in any appreciable numbers. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, I would remind the Minister of Finance, in case he has forgotten, that in the 1958 election campaign the present Prime
June 13, 1966

Minister promised that if elected his party would institute a program under which 2,500 scholarships and 7,500 bursaries would be provided every year for Canadian university students-not loans, but scholarships and bursaries. Then in the 1962 election campaign the present Prime Minister raised the ante with a promise to grant 10,000 scholarships, each worth $1,000, to students who wanted to attend university. It is a long time since we have heard anything about that promise of the Prime Minister. Instead we have this completely unsatisfactory student loans program.
What are the problems arising out of this program? I think they can be summarized very quickly. We believe that the welfare of this country, the rate at which this country will progress, is tied very closely to the kind of education we give to our young people. We believe that the whole university and technical school program in this country must be increased at a very substantial rate. We ought to recognize the fact that we are now in a period of crisis in higher education, that there are inadequate funds for university education and that until we solve that problem this country will continue to be in a period of crisis as far as higher education is concerned.
We are concerned about this. We are concerned about the financing of education. We believe that until this problem is solved the whole ability of this country to make the progress that is required will suffer. We believe that the cost of education must be met, not by the individual, not by the student and not by his parents but by the country as a whole, because the value to the country is a value to all its people. The value of increased and better education redounds to the benefit not only of the individuals concerned but to the country as a whole.
A number of careful studies have been made by universities, by departments of education, by the new manpower department, all of which indicate conclusively that there is a very substantial increase in the earning power of every person who attends university. We ought therefore to keep this in mind. It has been estimated that the person who attends university will earn, for every year he attended university, for the rest of his life an average of $1,000 a year more than if he had not attended university. The income tax alone that that person pays will more than repay the cost which the state, the people of Canada, invest in the education of those people who attend university.
Canada Student Loans Act
But the cost of attending university for a year is not just the cost of tuition, it is not just the cost of room and board-and that is very high for students who attend university in a city in which they do not live-it is not just the cost of books. There is the cost of lost earnings, and the cost of wages which are not earned while a student attends university. It has been estimated that the actual cost of attending university for a year is over $4,000. The estimate is based on living expenses of $1,000, tuition fees of $500 and $2,000 per year of lost earnings.
That being the case, it is obvious that a loans program in general is not the way to deal with this problem. Professor Seymour Harris, one of the most eminent American economists, has objected to this kind of student loans program for the following three reasons. First of all he says that people are not ready to purchase such an intangible asset on credit. Second, he says that the burden of debt will no doubt be discouraging to those who are the most needy already. Third, he says it is not certain that the Liberal scheme of loans will provide the educational opportunity which is claimed for them. The low tuition device has opened the door best to educational opportunity.
I suggest that the loans program-which has been successful, and the minister has indicated that something in the neighbourhood of
100,000	students have availed themselves of it in the two years since the program was commenced-helps those who need help the least, because it is the well-to-do who attend universities at the present time. Loans will make sure that this group will continue to attend university, while the children of people in the low income earning groups will not attend university. That is not surprising. It is not unusual in this day and age to have families in which there are two or three young people of university age who would like to attend university.
In connection with these young people $1,000 a year lent for four years means the incurring by the family of a debt in the neighbourhood of anything from $8,000 to $12,000, if they have two or three children. With interest this represents a debt in the neighbourhood of $15,000, because these loans have to be repaid at 6 per cent interest. The minister has done very well by the chartered banks of Canada. They will make money out of this program; you can be certain of that. Therefore it is not surprising that the children of parents in the low income brackets

The Canadian Union of Students, an organization which represents all university students in Canada, commissioned a survey of the incomes of parents of students attending university at the present time. This survey was sent to all members of parliament. Arising out of that survey, every member of parliament was circulated by letter from the Canadian Union of Students, signed by Patricia Horrobin, their associate secretary. I wish to quote a question which Miss Horrobin put to members of Parliament and to which I think the minister ought to give considerable thought. How long will 6 per cent of Canada's population, those who annually earn In excess of $10,000, send 25 per cent of all undergraduates to the 46 predominantly English speaking universities and colleges surveyed by the Canadian Union of Students? I submit, Mr. Chairman, that rather than solve the problem, the student loans program as proposed will worsen the situation of the Canadian Union of Students. that the students loan program will not only continue the situation but will aggravate it.

According to the survey, less than one-quarter of the Canadian population sends nearly half of all students to the 47 Canadian universities and colleges surveyed in February of 1965. Another two-thirds of the Canadian population, 64.1 per cent of the blue collar or working class status, in turn account for a little over a third of the university students, or 35 per cent. I submit that this is wrong and completely immoral. I suggest that instead of putting forward the student loans program the government should have introduced the very simple and practical program which the Prime Minister has proposed in his election campaigns, namely a program of
10,000	scholarships each worth $1,000. This program would help the young people who need most assistance.
The survey of which I have spoken indicates very clearly that by and large Canadian students do not represent the Canadian class structure but only the middle and upper income classes in Canadian society. An annual salary exceeding $10,000 is earned by 6.1 per cent of Canadian families, which provide 25 per cent of all university and college students in the surveyed institutions. I submit this situation is indefensible.
Families which earn annually less than $5,000, or 52 per cent of the Canadian population, provide slightly over 28 per cent of the students. Families earning less than $3,000 annually, or 22.1 per cent, provide only 9 per cent of the university population. The student loans program has done nothing and will do nothing to overcome these tremendous deficiencies.
Nearly one-fifth of all the students come from families in which the father is a university graduate, although only 5 per cent of Canadian heads of families graduated from the university-in other words four times the national population average. The student loans program will continue this terrible disparity. It will do nothing to make university education representative of the Canadian population as a whole.
The people who are most poorly represented in Canadian universities at the present time are the youngsters who come from rural homes. They do not get to university in appreciable numbers, or in any number comparable to their percentage of the total population. This has been the situation ever since universities began to function in Canada.

We have proposed that university education should be freely granted to every person who has the ability to attend. I suppose that this is too much to expect from the government and from Canadian society, which has always given to those who ask. I suggest that the time is long past when we could at least have expected that the very minimal proposals made by the government would have been implemented. I am referring to the proposals for scholarships made by the Prime Minister. Instead of that we are asked today to increase the amount of money available for students at the university level.
I said at the beginning and I say in closing that we will not vote against this resolution because this program is better than nothing at all. However it is a far cry from what the government has proposed and has promised to the people of Canada. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that if the government were to bring in the kind of legislation which has been promised so often, it would be passed in this house in time to be made available to students for the forthcoming university year. However, we have been told again and again that the government has no intention of proceeding with the kind of proposal made by the Prime Minister as long as eight years ago.
That being the case, as I said earlier we will vote for this resolution but we will only do so under protest and with the greatest of regret.

This report into the financing of higher education in Canada was published in 1965, and on page 30 is a table which should be of interest to us when we are considering the financing of higher university education.
This table, marked lx B, and headed, "Operating Income of Universities and Colleges," gives the percentage figures contributed to the operating costs of universities by fees, federal government contributions, provincial governments and others. This table, covering the decade 1954 to 1964, shows that the percentage contribution of fees has
June 13, 1966

Canada Student Loans Act changed almost not at all. In 1954 it was in the neighbourhood of 27 per cent, and at 1964 it still remained about 20 per cent of the operating income.
The percentage contribution of provincial governments began at the order of 40 per cent and remained at 40 per cent at the end of the decade. On the other hand, federal government contributions were of the order of 14 per cent to 15 per cent a decade ago and increased to 18 per cent and 19 per cent at the end of the ten year period, an increase of about 4 percentage points. Other contributions toward the operating income of universities from private individuals and private capital declined over the decade from 17 per cent to 14 per cent.
Let us examine what that means to us as a federal house when we are considering the voting of money toward assistance for students in universities. It means that the provincial governments have not changed the percentage contributions which they make to universities, and universities are provincial institutions. It means that the federal government has contributed more on a percentage basis, the addition being approximately equivalent to the amount by which private capital and private individuals have decreased their percentage contributions, thus helping to keep the fees percentage contribution steady.
In other words, federal money has tended to go into the treasuries of the provinces and not into the financing of higher education. Those of us who live close to universities know that when it comes time for a university to present its budget, usually it has to increase its annual budget to cope with the large and growing inflow of students. The university then has to go to the provincial government and each year ask for higher amounts.
The provincial government estimates what will be the size of the federal contribution, finds out whether the per capita grant has increased, whether the Canada Council is helping with the cost of capital construction and finally, when it has reckoned what the federal contribution will be, it says to the university, "We cannot grant you the budget you ask for expanding higher education in this province this year, and we are going to cut your budget back seriously." The provincial government puts on the squeeze, and the federal contribution tends to flow indirectly into the general revenues of the province
[Mr. Deachman.l
rather than into assistance to higher education.
When we as a federal house contemplate higher education and its assistance, when we are considering assistance to students by way of loans or by direct grant, scholarship or research, or when we are considering per capita grants or construction grants through the Canada Council or C.M.H.C., we must ask ourselves how we can work out a device to assist higher education, and which at the same time does not tend to subsidize the general revenues of the provinces.
This is a serious problem that faces a federal government when it spends dollars in the field of higher education. I do not really know what can be done about it, but at the undergraduate level we must move more and more toward assistance to the student, and at the postgraduate level we must move more towards programs of research, programs of higher scholarship-in other words, fellowships and doctorates-and toward the provision of research equipment, so that the end product of the research laboratories of universities and the scholars which they produce tend to benefit the nation.
By doing this at the postgraduate level we can produce a higher yield, and by doing it at the undergraduate level we shall assist the student rather than the university itself, which is a provincial institution. In this way, as time goes on we should be able to direct federal dollars to better purposes in the higher education of Canadians.

He said: the present bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act is virtually identical to that presented to the house a year ago but which lapsed when the last session of parliament ended. Today I shall explain some of the major amendments that are contained in the bill. Some of these are very closely related to certain provisions in the bill to revise the Bank Act, which will be introduced very shortly, and it will therefore be necessary for me to indicate what we intend to propose in that regard. It is, of course, the intention to refer both the bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act and the new Bank Act to the standing committee of finance, trade and economic affairs so that members may have the opportunity to study all the proposed changes carefully.
One of the major changes that is proposed in the bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act is a new section which will clarify the relationship between the government of Canada and the Bank of Canada in regard to the responsibility for monetary policy. This section accomplishes two purposes. First, it makes clear there must be, as there is now, continuous consultation on monetary policy between the government and the bank. Second, it provides a formal procedure whereby, in the event of a disagreement between

June 13, 1966
Bank of Canada Act
the government and the bank which cannot be resolved, the government may, after further consultation has taken place, issue a directive to the bank as to the monetary policy that is to follow. Any such directive must be in writing, must be in specific terms, and must be applicable for a specified period. This new section requires that the directive be published forwith in the Canada Gazette and that it be tabled in parliament within fifteen days. Another proposed change that is closely related to this new section is the elimination of the power which the governor was given in the original act, but which has never been used, to veto any action or decision of the board of directors or of the executive committee of the bank.
Members will recognize that the objective of the proposed new section, which follows the recommendation of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, is to remove any doubt which may ever have existed about the responsibilities of the government and the bank for monetary policy. Under the proposed legislation it will not be possible for the government to deny its ultimate responsibility for the monetary policy which is followed, any more than it can in any other field of national policy.
A most important feature of the proposed amendment is that if the government exercises its right to insist on a charge in monetary policy, it will be required to do so openly, that is, in a way which brings the issue to the attention of parliament and the public. At the same time there is nothing in the proposed arrangements which in any way relieves the bank and the governor of their responsibilities for monetary policy and its execution. If the government of the day ever issued a directive to the governor of the day to execute a monetary policy which he felt was contrary to the public interest, it can be presumed that he would resign rather than accept such a responsibility.
I should like to stress that the intent of the proposed amendment is not to change the basis of the existing relationship between the government and the bank, which is based on these general principles and is working well in practice, but rather to give it clear legislative recognition. In this connection, it may be recalled that the present governor of the bank at the time of his appointment publicly expressed views regarding this matter of responsibility which are consistent with the principles proposed by the royal commission and embodied in the proposed amendment.
{Mr. Sharp.]
I should like now to refer to the changes which are being proposed in this bill, and that it is intended to propose in the bill to amend the Bank Act, in the cash and secondary reserve requirements of the chartered banks. At the present time the minimum average cash reserve requirement of the chartered banks is 8 per cent of the Canadian dollar deposit liabilities calculated on a daily average basis for each calendar month. Members will recall that in the Bank Act presented last year it was proposed to reduce the percentage from 8 per cent to 7 per cent gradually.
When the bill to amend the Bank Act is introduced shortly the intention is to contain an amendment which will set a minimum cash reserve requirement of 12 per cent against deposit liabilities payable on demand in Canadian dollars, plus a minimum requirement of 4 per cent of deposit liabilities payable after notice in Canadian dollars. On the basis of the present distribution of the deposit liabilities of the banks the over-all result of the new proposal would not differ greatly from the previous one since the over-all ratio, that is, the ratio of required cash reserves to total Canadian dollar deposits, would work out to about 6.6 per cent. However, the proposed change which accepts in principle a recommendation of the royal commission would place the banks in a position where they may compete with other financial institutions on more equal terms for savings and time deposits. Provision is made for a gradual shift to the new cash reserve basis. It is also intended to propose that the period over which daily cash reserves are averaged for the purpose of meeting the requirement should be reduced from one month to half a month. These particular proposals will be contained in the bill to amend the Bank Act.
That bill will also propose that the Bank of Canada be given a stand-by power, within certain limits and subject to certain notice requirements, to impose a minimum secondary reserve requirement, the secondary reserves to consist of notes of and deposits with the Bank of Canada in excess of the cash reserve requirement which I have just outlined, together with treasury bills and day-to-day loans. The present bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act gives the Bank of Canada the power to vary this secondary reserve requirement. Should the Bank of Canada find it necessary to invoke the power to impose and vary the secondary reserve requirement, the bank could not set the initial requirement at more than 6 per cent of
June 13, 1966

total Canadian dollar deposit liabilities and could not increase it by more than one per cent per month. In no case could the required ratio exceed 12 per cent. At the present time, by agreement with the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks maintain a secondary reserve of at least 7 per cent, in conjunction with the 8 per cent cash reserve. The stand-by power to impose and vary a minimum secondary reserve requirement would replace the present power of the Bank of Canada to vary the minimum cash ratio, which will be removed by this bill. It has proven in practice to be of little use and we think the variable secondary reserve would be more practical.
The proposed stand-by power would provide a means of impounding or releasing chartered bank liquidity, which in turn would have an influence on bank lending policies, and it would supplement the more usual technique of changing the amount of cash reserves available to the banks in relation to the minimum requirement. The raising or lowering of secondary reserve requirements can exert this influence with less impact on interest rates, a technique which could have important advantages in some instances, particularly those in which it might be necessary to have regard to the effect of changes in interest rates on capital flows into or out of Canada. This is not an unusual power for a central bank. The Bank of England has the power to call up special deposits, which is equivalent to raising secondary reserve requirements, and the Federal Reserve Board has the power to vary cash reserve requirements of commercial banks.

There are several sections which have been in the Bank of Canada Act since 1934 but which have long been inoperative. The Royal Commission on Banking and Finance recommended that these be removed and in this bill it is proposed to follow that recommendation. One of these sections covers the power of the Bank of Canada to act as banker or fiscal agent of the government of a province; this power has never been used and it would be difficult to exercise in a manner consistent with the bank's statutory responsibility in the field of monetary policy and as fiscal agent of the government of Canada.
Another such section is the one which requires the bank to maintain a reserve of gold and foreign exchange against its note and deposit liabilities and to redeem its notes in gold on demand. This section ceased to have any practical meaning after the bank's
Bank of Canada Act
holdings of gold and its holdings of foreign exchange, other than working balances, were transferred to the government's exchange fund in 1940.
In a related amendment it is proposed to remove the description "payable to bearer on demand" in respect of notes of the Bank of Canada. Since these notes are themselves legal tender under the terms of the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act and have never in fact been convertible into gold, the present wording is archaic, unnecessary and I am sure as puzzling to the members of the house as it has been to me for years.
In accordance with recommendations of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance the bill contains several provisions which affect the existing arrangements regarding directors and management of the Bank of Canada. Partners, officers or employees of firms of investment dealers which act as primary distributors of government of Canada securities would be added to the list of those ineligible for appointment to the bank's board of directors, on the ground that their business activities involve direct dealings with the central bank. The membership of the bank's executive committee would be enlarged by the appointment of an additional director, and the aggregate annual amount of directors' fees would be raised in order to permit more frequent meetings of the full board. It is also proposed that certain pension provisions relating to the governor and the deputy governor be made subject to the approval of the governor in council, as their appointment and salary now are.
Hon. members might find it helpful if I were to draw their attention to the one change that has been made in this bill from the version that was presented a year ago, and that is a minor provision that lengthens from 14 days to 21 days the period that may elapse between the date on which the minister receives the annual accounts of the bank and the governor's annual report, and the date on which these documents must be tabled in parliament. The sole purpose of this change is to allow adequate time for translation and printing.
There is one other provision relating to the Bank of Canada which it is intended to propose in the new Bank Act which I should mention at this time. This would give the Bank of Canada power to require information from the chartered banks provided that the banks shall not be required to furnish information with respect to the accounts of an individual customer. This section is included

June 13, 1966
Bank of Canada Act
in the Bank Act simply because that act includes all other provisions dealing with bank returns.
Provisions of the bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act which I have not touched on involve a number of relatively minor technical matters. Hon. members will have the opportunity of considering them in detail in committee along with the matters that I have mentioned today.
While we are on the subject of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the way in which monetary policy has developed in recent years. It has been, I believe, consistently directed toward the encouragement of sustained economic growth, while at the same time taking full account of the need to maintain a sound external financial position. Although the central bank has had to contend with some special factors arising out of our own balance of payments problems and those of the United States, as well as a difficult situation last summer following the default of a major finance company, I believe the basic monetary policy followed has been clearly apparent. So long as the economy was operating under a general condition in which unused resources were available to be drawn into production, monetary policy allowed growing demands for credit to be met without any tightening of credit conditions.
Over the past year or so, however, as the amount of slack in the economy decreased and as we drew closer to the limits of our productive capacity, which fortunately is growing, it became necessary to permit rising demands for credit to have an impact on credit conditions. I recognize that in some areas of the country a certain amount of slack remains, and that these situations continue to require attention, but taking the economy as a whole there has for some time been little capacity to spare. This situation has been reflected in low unemployment rates, rapid growth of employment, shortages of many kinds of skilled workers, rising prices and costs and a high level of imports. In these circumstances, it would not be in the public interest to encourage generally easy credit conditions. At a time when the economy is operating close to its physical limits easy money could only put additional upward pressure on prices and costs.
The fact that credit is now somewhat more difficult to obtain and interest rates are higher is therefore a reflection of the high level of

economic activity and prosperity in this country. The upward adjustment of interest rates has not been a development limited to Canada; they have followed a similar trend in the United States. Indeed there has been a general rise in interest rates throughout the western world, which reflects the high level of economic activity in most countries and the widespread demand for capital.
I believe that it is essential that we follow policies that are designed to moderate inflationary pressures and thereby improve our opportunity for sustained growth. I believe, however, that monetary policy should not have to carry a disproportionate share of this burden, and in fact it could not do so successfully. The measures announced in the budget, in combination with monetary policy and the other economic policies of this government, will provide a mix of policies which, in the opinion of the government, is appropriate to our present economic circumstances and prospects.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I shall speak for only a few minutes in order to allow the maximum number of hon. members to participate, so that we may get as much of the opinion of the house on this motion as is feasible. Discussion of such a motion is not something new, and in dealing with it I shall refer to excerpts from Hansard to show the importance that was attributed to it by hon. members on previous occasions.
Much discussion has taken place in the past concerning the method of appointments to the Senate. The electorate of the country has exerted pressure to have changes made in the manner of making appointments-even going as far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would go, in seeking the complete abolition of that part of parliament. I sincerely believe that the other place has contributed and does contribute a great deal to the welfare of Canada and to the general benefit of Canadians.
I do not believe it should be abolished, but in this connection I would like to refer to the importance placed on this matter by the official opposition some years ago, when I first entered parliament. The importance of it was emphasized by amendments moved to motions to go into supply. At page 5245 of the 1954 Hansard, Mr. Drew, the then leader of the opposition moved:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"the government should give consideration to initiating the necessary consultation and inquiry respecting reform of the Senate so that all appropriate steps may be taken, including such matters as the method by which the members of the Senate should be chosen and their tenure of office, so that the Senate may more effectively discharge the constitutional function it was intended to serve as an integral part of our parliamentary system.

At page 5335 of Hansard for 1955 Mr. Rowe moved a similar amendment:
The government should give consideration to initiating the necessary consultation and inquiry respecting reform of the Senate so that all appropriate steps may be taken, including such matters as the method by which the members of the Senate should be chosen and their tenure of office, so that the Senate may more effectively discharge the constitutional function it was intended to serve as an integral part of our parliamentary system.
The present Premier of Saskatchewan, Mr. Thatcher, had this to say on the matter, as recorded at page 5338 of Hansard for 1955:
I am not going to take the time of the house to go into the weaknesses of the Senate. They can be summed up very briefly. Members are appointed rather than elected; appointments appear to have been made as a reward for past political services instead of any particular ability.
The late former minister of finance in the Conservative government, Mr. Nowlan, had this to say as recorded at page 5254 of Hansard for 1954:
The Prime Minister is also the leader of the government of this country, and a man whom we all respect although we may disagree with him on many of the policies that he advocates from time to time. As the leader of the government of this country he has the direct responsibility for changing the situation whereby one arm of this parliament is now rapidly falling into disrepute, if not contempt. It is a situation, sir, that cannot be allowed to continue. Certainly the time has come when something definite must be done.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) published a pamphlet in 1962, and I quote the following paragraphs from the last page of it:
The Senate should not be a device to reward party faithful for past favours, or for getting rid of a minister whose presence in the cabinet is no longer desirable. Here is where the room for reform lies . . .
Regardless of which party will win the next election, I express the hope that the Prime Minister of the day will embark on a new policy with regard to the appointments to the Senate, and let that body continue to do the useful job which they are now performing within the limits imposed on it.

I can honestly say that since I came to this house I was never more disappointed than when I looked at the list of the appointments made recently to the other place. That is no reflection on the individuals themselves, but the reason why they were appointed was apparent to everybody in the country.

Without meaning any offence to my good friend the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe), I must say I have never heard him explain why he advocates setting up ten commissions, instead of five, or one, for that matter. I thought he would have adhered to his notice of motion. I am forced, however, to make a few comments on some of his remarks, because personally I do not see the purpose or the necessity of setting up ten provincial commissions, plus a federal commission, to sit together and suggest Senate appointments to the government.
I think it has become common practice to criticize people appointed to the other place, as if the fact of having been long active in politics, a party contributor or treasurer would transform appointees into wretched persons or persons unfit to appear in public.
I should like merely to endorse the comments made by Senator O'Leary, who is certainly not a Liberal senator, when he said on June 2, 1965, as reported on page 192 of the Debates of the Senate:
Honourable senators, I have been reading, during the past two weeks, the convocation addresses of eminent persons before our various universities; and almost invariably these men stressed the need to get young Canadians interested in public life. They pleaded with students to go out and get into the dusty arena of practical politics and thus to help serve their country.
But, honourable senators, according to the Toronto Star's editorial, which has been repeated again and again in the press of Canada during the past three or four weeks, when it comes to appointing persons to this house, politicians are to be regarded as lepers and the house is to be filled with musicians, sculptors, painters, and so on, Honourable senators, that is nonsense.
In concluding, he said the following:
I repeat that, when I quit this Senate, whoever may be prime minister I hope he replaces me by a good staunch party man who has worked at party politics, and not by a man who, as I said is good at music or sculpturing.
Mr. Speaker, the more I listened to the hon. member, the more I realized that people seem to be unaware that, from the very beginning of confederation, it was provided that regions would be represented. Is it necessary to recall that Canada is divided into territorial divisions: 24 senators for Quebec, 24 for Ontario, 24 for the western Provinces, 24 for the Maritimes and six for the province of Newfoundland.

June 13, 1966
The Senate
Mr. Speaker, I fail to see why, in 1966, in an extremely difficult political period for Canada, we should try to divide this country more and more into areas. If we, in the House of Commons, are about to suggest that the Senate should reflect somewhat our own image, I wonder what would be the usefulness of the second house, namely the Senate.
If we are going to ask that all provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Quebec or the Maritimes, etc. be represented exactly as they are in the provincial political field, I think we would then have a mere duplication of what already exists.
I have no doubt that if we asked that each region be represented according to the party in power, we would only encourage divisiveness in Canada. We know the member of parliament must not limit his interests to his riding. I am to some extent defining my own role as member, and I know I was elected to represent my riding. But I assure you that when I come to the House of Commons, I want to represent more than the limited interests of my riding, I want to take an interest in all that goes on throughout Canada, whether in Alberta, British Columbia, or elsewhere; in fact I feel that where things Canadian are concerned, I too should have my say, just like my good friend who preceded me can do as concerns the province of Quebec. I recognize his right, as he does mine, to discuss what happens in Quebec as well as in the prairies.
And I believe the same applies to some extent for senators. They are chosen by a man who was elected by the Canadian people, namely the prime minister. I find it more and more difficult to understand why attempts are made to remove from the people elected by the people such prerogratives as they hold through the constitution. As soon as a Prime Minister has the least bit of latitude, the least prerogative, in short as soon as he is given some authority, you hear at once that those powers should be delegated to groups, organizations, representatives who, in my opinion, are far less represnetative than the right hon. Prime Minister of the country himself. And, in this case, there is no doubt that it is the prerogative of the Prime Minister to appoint the members of the Senate.
Now, what will the Prime Minister do with this prerogative which he has? If that Prime Minister is a wise man-and I believe it will be in the interest of a Prime Minister, who is the leader of a party, to make appointments that will not be too unpleasant-and if he has a political sense, he will see to it that the

appointments he makes are as profitable as possible, as far as the national interest is concerned, and he will choose the most qualified people. I could not understand a prime minister having a personal prerogative under the constitution to nominate people to the other house or to key positions who would appoint people unqualified for these responsibilities. I cannot undertand this insistence, when you make a rather thorough survey of all the appointments or when you simply consult the Parliamentary Guide and read the biography of each of the honourable senators.

I think the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) is to be commended for placing this motion before the house today. I say this, not so much because I agree with the principle of his motion-I will say at the outset that I do not-but because I think that it is useful for all those who are interested in the development of our system of parliamentary government to discuss, to consider and to investigate proposals for the change of our parliamentary institutions, proposals aimed at making them work better and more effectively. I will say, however, Mr. Speaker, that my view, which I hope to put forward more extensively in the next few moments, is that the adoption of the proposal contained in this motion will not make our system of parliamentary government at the federal level work more effectively, but that it will do just the opposite.
Let us go back to the time of the Fathers of Confederation and look briefly at the reasons for establishing not only an elected House of Commons but also an appointed upper house, a Senate. I think it will be found that basically there were four reasons for the institution of the Senate in the initial structure of the new Canadian nation. First, I think it is clear that at that time there was a fear of the concept of democracy-a fear of the concept of the operation of the popular will.
Second, I think there was at that time a feeling that there needed to be some special form of protection of the institution of property, some special voice in the parliamentary system for property interests. Third, I think it was felt there was a need for some manner of protecting special privileges; I do not mean privileges of regions so much as privileges of classes or social groups in the operation of the parliamentary system. Fourth, a need was

felt for the protection of provincial and regional interests.
Whatever the Fathers of Confederation may have felt about the validity of these four arguments, I think that we in this house will agree that our views today are quite different on these points from what they were over a hundred years ago. There may still be some people, but there could not be very many, who accept the idea that the ordinary man-the so-called common man, if there is such a thing-is not fit to pass judgment and to make decisions on how his own affairs should be conducted. I think it is pretty well accepted that the ordinary man is quite capable, through his vote and through other means available to him of approaching his government through his elected representatives or even more directly of putting forward his views and expressing his ideas on how our government should be run.
I also think we have given up the idea that there is need for a special form of protection in our parliamentary system for the institution of private property. I think this problem, if there ever was one, has been largely eliminated by the evolution of an economic and social system which makes it possible for the ordinary man to acquire property in ways that the Fathers of Confederation would be amazed to see. They would be amazed to see, for example, to what extent factory workers acquire their own cars, their own homes and in those homes all sorts of appliances which, whatever value they may have or whatever effect they may have on our pace of life, are certainly such that the ordinary man today has as much a stake in the existence of this country as had any landed proprietor of over 100 years ago who felt that his property rights needed some special protection against what he then considered to be the uninformed approaches of the ordinary man. We have certainly rejected long ago the idea that certain economic or social groups need special protection through the institution of an upper house.
There remains then for us to examine the concept that provincial or regional interests need to have some special form of expression through a chamber of our parliamentary system. I think it is clear today that for various reasons the provinces have been put into the position of being able to take care of themselves without the need of special protection provided by a body of a national parliament created to give them or their representatives
June 13, 1966

some particular voice. Over the years between confederation and the beginning of the second world war, the courts, and especially the British privy council did an all-too-effec-tive job of constructing a framework of protection beyond what many others intended, including I feel even the Fathers of Confederation. I think it is clear, whether we all agree or not, that this certainly extended the powers and the role of the provinces beyond even the extensive powers they were given in the clear words of the British North America Act. The decisions in particular of the British privy council, which was then the final court of resort for Canadians, gave the provinces such power in many areas of economic and social policy that today the federal government is not in the position to act in these areas without the agreement or at least the co-operation of the provinces.
The provinces also have always found their premiers, their cabinets and their provincial assemblies quite willing to assert themselves and their own point of view. I think that because of the willingness, the ability and in fact the strong desire of provincial leaders to assert their ideas in the national sphere, there appears to be no real need for spokesmen for provincial interests in a body such as the Senate of Canada. Our means of communication today provide for direct contact with the federal cabinet, the Prime Minister and his ministers in ways undreamt of one hundred years ago. The Fathers of Confederation could hardly have been expected to consider that it would be possible for the premier of British Columbia, for example, to pick up a telephone and speak to a federal cabinet minister, or to the Prime Minister of Canada himself, on some matter of concern to the province of British Columbia.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
Perhaps even more important, as a means of permitting provinces and their leaders to put forward their points of view, has been the development of the federal-provincial conference. Concern has been expressed in this house and elsewhere over the implications of the growth of the institution of the federal-provincial conference one hundred years ago. It is clear that the growth and de-velompent of the concept of the federal-provincial conference, not just as an occasional meeting taking place on an irregular basis every few years but on an almost month-to-month basis in our national structure, involving meetings not only between members
The Senate
of the cabinets of the provinces and the federal government but people at the official level both provincially and federally, as well has I think eliminated the need which the Fathers of Confederation might have been seen over 100 years ago for the use of the Senate as a place where provincial and regional voices need to be heard.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the putting into effect of the idea contained in the resolution of the hon. member for Cariboo would do much to weaken the ability of the federal government as a national entity to make decisions and to implement these decisions in the interests of Canada as a nation.
There are those who feel there has already been a trend away from the federal government and toward the provinces in the matter of decision making. I am not going to enter into this subject this afternoon because it is one to which we could devote not only this private members hour, but whole days of discussion. Nevertheless I certainly feel there is need for a strong and effective government which can operate on a national basis across Canada to deal with problems which, whatever they may have been in the day of the Fathers of Confederation, can be effectively dealt with today, in my view at least, only on a national basis.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Cariboo spoke critically of the method of appointment and of the calibre of Senators appointed at the present time.

I thank the hon. member for Cariboo for that intervention because I think it leads very well to the point I was about to attempt to make. I think the hon. member's intervention will illustrate even better perhaps than I could myself the idea which I am trying to get across to the members of this chamber.
Is there any certainty that the putting into effect of the hon. member's suggestion would bring into the Senate of Canada people who have ability and a record of achievement which is more impressive than those who are there at the present time? The hon. member

June 13, 1966
The Senate
for Cariboo has just suggested-and I thank him for this suggestion-that good people are to be found throughout the country, and I agree with him. If it is true that this is being done-and I am not saying that I accept this concept-then why would provincial premiers be any the less likely to reward political service or to find a place for those who have served their province in one capacity or another by recommending them for appointment to the Senate of Canada?

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member again, but at no time did I mention any provincial premier.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
I am not saying that provincial premiers will make appointments, but certainly the hon. member speaks in his motion of setting up provincial commissions consisting of representatives appointed by each province. Now, who would appoint these representatives if it were not the provincial premiers? And what would these commissions represent if it were not the viewpoints of the provincial premiers holding office from time to time? I suggest to the house that no reason has been advanced to show that the criteria which would be used by these commissions would operate any differently from the criteria used at the present time for the appointment of people to the Senate of Canada.
At least, Mr. Speaker, those who are being appointed today are those who have some sense of responsibility toward the concept of a national federal state for Canada, of the Canadian nation as an entity, instead of just a weak confederation of provinces. At least, Mr. Speaker, the method we use today will avoid the possibility of having a group of senators who would obstruct or block legislation because they are more concerned with putting forward a narrow regional or provincial view than with supporting something which would benefit a great nation of Canada stretching from ocean to ocean.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is assuming that today senators are not appointed from the various provinces. Of course they are. It is the method of appointment to which I am drawing attention. The hon. member is getting away from the issue.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: Today there is a kind of limited way of narrowing or limiting this risk because people appointed to the Senate have usually been active in some form of public life, and have had an opportunity to develop some sense of responsibility.

speechtext: As defeated candidates?

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: Perhaps as defeated candidates. The senators develop some sense of responsibility similar to that developed by representatives actually elected by and responsible to the people.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS

speechtext:
I thank the house for its indulgence. I know that some hon. members for whom I have the greatest respect do not agree Quite obviously with what I am trying to put forward.
Even though senators do not have to face the public through the vote, and even though there is no way of recalling them, they do form part of their party groups, and attend the caucuses of their parties. They are able to develop a certain sense of moral obligation if you like and this applies whether a senator's party is in office or not.
Because it is argued that senators, in a democratic way, are not accountable to the people through elections, it is argued by some that the appointments to positions of senators should go to scholars, artists, and those completely outside political life in this country.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that we should not confuse the concept of the need for a sort of legion of honour with the need for a legislative body. If there is a need to more openly recognize our scholars, artists and poets, and perhaps there is, then let us do that. Let us do it through a concept similar to the French legion of honour. Let us not confuse the need of honoring people in the intellectual and academic sphere with the need for setting up another sort of legislative body. Intellectuals and scholars may never have had a real link with or great concern for the public. Even
The Senate
though candidates are defeated they will not have-and I see the hon. member for Anti-gonish-Guysborough and I do not mean this personally-the sort of intellectual arrogance occasionally seen which stems from not having their views tested in the popular marketplace of an election.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
