speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: I notice that the proposal is for provincial governments to participate in the selection of members of the Senate. I want to ask the hon. gentleman if the adoption of this motion, and the putting of it into effect, might not encourage a multiplicity of parties in this country, an effect damaging to parliamentary democracy as we know it.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: This is a good point.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: I must say that the way to eliminate the multiplicity of parties in this country is for those who do not agree with that concept to so conduct themselves through their policies that the people will not be interested in voting for any other party than the one carrying out the policies. It is true, none the less, that multiplicity of parties has created problems for sound and effective parliamentary government. Those who support minority parties create the risk of bringing about certain forms of weakness in the abilities of governments to act firmly and effectively in the national interest.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PROCEDURE IN MAKING APPOINTMENTS
speechtext: A very good point.

speechtext:
With respect to the argument advanced by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe), that his proposal would reflect views expressed by the ballot box, I submit that in provincial elections the people are directing their thoughts only to electing a government to carry out the administration of their province. Not to any other issue. If the hon. member is serious in his argument, let him support the concept of an elected Senate. If the people wish to elect a senator from his party or from some other minority party, even though this may be detrimental to effective national government, they could do so.
I do not think the hon. member's argument is sound in support of his motion. I therefore ask hon. members of this house to reject it. May I call it seven o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Sharp for the second reading of Bill No. C-190 to amend the Bank of Canada Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
At the
adjournment at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was indicating our doubts as to the efficacy of the policies for the guidance of the economy represented by higher interest rates, and those concerned with the global totals of the currency. As I said, that has an indiscriminate effect and therefore is discriminatory against the small borrowers, whether they are small businessmen or small individual borrowers.
I think the most important section of the bill before us concerns the relationship of the government to the policies pursued by the Bank of Canada. I have very grave doubts as to whether the particular provision of the bill that has been placed before the house by the Minister of Finance carries out the purpose which we should all have in mind, namely that monetary policy is essentially government policy and not that of the Bank of Canada.
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I begin by reminding hon. members of the preamble of the Bank of Canada Act as it is found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952.
Whereas it is desirable to establish a central bank in Canada to regulate credit and currency-
I draw the attention of the house to the following words:
-in the best interests of the economic life of the nation-
I continue quoting:
-to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level-
I ask the house to note the following words:
__of production, trade, prices and employment,
so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare of the Dominion.
What this preamble means, and what in fact monetary policy relates to, is the entire 
economy of the country. When the Bank of Canada was set up by Prime Minister Bennett-the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) mentioned with some pride the fact that Mr. Bennett introduced the Bank of Canada Act-the proposal of the then prime minister in 1935 was a proposal to make the Bank of Canada a privately-owned bank which was none the less to be a central bank. This was mistaken, and in 1936 the minister of finance, Mr. Dunning, and the Liberal government of that day recognized the fact that the Bank of Canada was dealing with policies which affected the entire economy and could not be separated from government control.
My first proposition, and there is nothing original about it, is that there has been undesirable confusion about the part played by the Bank of Canada in connection with the operation of policy, requiring technical knowledge, and that part which is concerned with the initiation and implementation of monetary policy. We have frequently taken the attitude in Canada that, because the technical operations of the bank must necessarily be left to technicians, the making of policy by the Bank of Canada should also be an independent process. This, in my respectful submission, is sheer nonsense. The Minister of Finance in his proposal in this bill, if he will forgive me for saying so, carries on the same nonsensical myth. What he proposes is that normally there should be consultation between the minister and the governor of the bank. Should a difference of opinion arise then the minister may, by order in council, tell the Bank of Canada what to do. But he must specify the thing to be done and specify the term during which his instruction is to last.
This carries forward the undesirable concept that the Bank of Canada is some sort of independent body which has independent authority to make monetary policy for Canada. I assume that the clause before us is concerned not with the technical carrying out of a particular policy but the making of policy, the decision as to what policy should in fact be carried out.
This is my submission. I do not say this dogmatically but nevertheless I do so with some conviction. Monetary policy itself is entirely, not partially but entirely, the responsibility of the government. The Minister of Finance at any time must be able to say what this policy should be and the governor of the Bank of Canada must be by law
June 13, 1966

obliged to carry that policy into effect by whatever technical means he may think advisable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: I am very interested in the hon. member's views. May I ask whether he thinks it would be desirable in the event of a difference of view about monetary policy that the public at large should be aware of it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
Not necessarily. I imagine there are other ways of making the public at large aware of what is happening. What the public at large is interested in is the nature of the policy, not the fact that the minister and the governor of the bank have a difference of opinion. I believe the public at large could not care less, and I do not think it is of the slightest importance whether or not the minister and the governor agree or disagree. What is important is that we should know what the policy of the government is.
I can see no reason why the minister should not be able to control the policy as it affects the monetary system of the economy in the same way as he controls fiscal policy. We become tied by tradition. I support this is true of all people at all times and in all places. We become sold on an idea and cannot get rid of it. The fact is that the minister's decisions on taxation policy are just as important as decisions on monetary policy. Frequently, indeed, they have a more direct effect on the economy. When the bank rate is increased and the interest rate rises in consequence there is usually a time lag before the effect is felt. But a tax revision, whether upward or downward, invariably has an immediate effect on the economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting that every activity of the central bank in the market should be subject to parliamentary approval, such as a decision to buy some government securities or sell them?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister's question enables me to illustrate what I have said much more clearly than I have done so far. His question is related to a direct operation to implement a policy. If it were decided by the minister that the interest rate should go up and that the currency available should be contracted, then there are certain operations which the Bank of Canada may carry out in order to achieve this purpose. Certain other steps could be taken to achieve an opposite purpose. This is a technical operation of the bank and the minister does not have to interfere with it at all. It is his responsibility,
Bank of Canada Act
and when I say this I mean the responsibility of the government and himself, to determine whether or not it is right at any given time for the amount of currency to be constricted and for the interest rate to go up in order that certain purposes may be achieved. Such decisions should not be left to the governor of the bank to be taken at his own discretion.
This has been argued in Canada over the years. When the late Mr. Dunning, minister of finance in 1936, introduced the act which made the Bank of Canada a publicly owned institution he spoke as follows, and I commend these words to the minister. They are to be found in the 1936 Hansard at page 3260:
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
-the matter of public ownership is in my opinion much less important than that of governmental control. If we study the constitution of central banks from this aspect we shall find ample precedent for the attempt which we are making to give the government adequate control over the Bank of Canada.
In 1956 Hon. Donald Fleming agreed with this but, despite what the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said, when Mr. Fleming became minister of finance he stated, as recorded at pages 3098 and 3099 of Hansard for April 27, 1959:
I wish to make it quite clear that the government, as such, does not exercise control over the money supply or over the amount of money in circulation.
Further on he said:
-I would point out that in the matter of monetary policy this parliament has placed the responsibility and indeed the power in the hands of the Bank of Canada. The government does not exercise any sway in the field of monetary policy.
I think Mr. Fleming was wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext: So do I.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
In a speech broadcast by the C.B.C. on October 1, 1959, the present Leader of the Opposition said:
I should point out that the Bank of Canada, not the government, controls the money supply in Canada.
Let me interject that there again is the confusion between the technical operations which do the controlling and the policy decision as to whether there should be control and in what directions that control should be exercised. The Leader of the Opposition went on to say in that speech:
The bank was set up under law by act of parliament. It is independent and autonomous. It has one master, though: parliament, and through parliament the people.

June 13, 1966
Bank of Canada Act
If it was that, and I really doubt if that was a statement of fact at that time, it was wrongly independent and autonomous.
My point is this, Mr. Speaker. We have reached in our economy, as have other countries, a situation of complexity which everybody now agrees requires an amount of planning by government which economies in the past did not require from the point of view of hon. gentlemen opposite and of those to my right. Personally I belong to a school of thought that has always believed our economy cannot serve the interests of the people without direct and conscious government planning of the direction in which the economy should go at any given time. But now the idea of planning is universally accepted and, whether members believe 50 per cent or 100 per cent in planning, one way or another there is hardly a member of the house who denies the basic proposition.
Some 30 years ago when I first became active in public life people denied government planning. They said it was wrong for governments to plan, but now every member of the house acknowledges the fact that government planning is necessary. I disagreed with the minister's budget. I thought what he tried to do was inadequate but none the less what he tried to do was to plan the economy from the fiscal point of view, to have certain fiscal policies which in his view would be adequate to meet what he thought were inflationary pressures in the economy.
I say that just as important as fiscal policy is the monetary policy of the country, the financial policy. I say that even the clauses which are before us in this bill, despite what the minister said, do not make it sufficiently clear that the monetary policy is his and not that of the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Essentially the minister says in this bill: I consult with him but if he disagrees with me I can override him.
I say that this bill ought to make it clear that monetary policy basically and at all times is the responsibility of the government, that it is the minister who decides what that policy ought to be, that it is the Bank of Canada which advises him, in the same way as many other people advise him, and that it is the Bank of Canada which carries that policy into effect through the technical operations which are required.
It is not sufficient to say that if the minister disagrees with the governor then certain steps will be followed. Indeed, it seems to me to be wrong in principle to suggest that each

time the minister is in disagreement with the Governor of the Bank of Canada this will happen. I suggest to hon. members that that will be a deterrent to this or any other minister insisting on his policy because in order to insist on the policy which the government considers to be right he will have to say to the governor: Look, fellow, I am going to order you to do this. If the governor is a man of ideas, a man of principles and selfrespect, all of which and perhaps a great deal more is true of the present governor of the bank, then the governor will say to the minister: You do it without me; I am going home; you can have my resignation.
If the minister is faced each time with the likelihood of the resignation of the Governor of the Bank of Canada I suggest that nine times out of ten the minister will bend his policy in order to avoid both the economic and political consequences of the resignation of the governor of the bank. There is no need for this at all. There is no reason in the world why the legislation should not clearly spell out that monetary policy is the responsibility of the government and that the Governor of the Bank of Canada must always implement the policy decided upon by the government and the Minister of Finance. If you spell that out as a regular part of the routine of the bank, then the kind of difficulty I have indicated would invariably follow a difference of opinion between the two would be obviated. I say again that I cannot imagine any minister of finance insisting on his policy being carried out in the face of the likely resignation of the governor of the bank unless the difference is so tremendous that he is willing to risk the consequences of such resignation.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I question the philosophy behind our attitude to the Bank of Canada up until now and even the philosophy behind the amendment which the minister has proposed. I do not deny it is an amendment which will make the situation much better in that it sets out government responsibility more clearly than was the case hitherto, but it still accepts a falacious philosphy that the monetary policy of the country is something that should be given to an outside body as its responsibility to evolve, even though in consultation with the minister and that it is only in an exceptional case that the minister can impose his will on the governor. This is a false understanding of monetary policy.
June 13, 1966

There is not a branch of the economy that is not affected by the monetary policy initiated and implemented by the Bank of Canada. There is not a branch of the economy that is not affected when the Bank of Canada increases interest rates. There is not a branch of the economy that is not affected when the Bank of Canada increases or decreases the amount of money available. There is not a branch of the economy that is not affected by the action of the Bank of Canada when it insists on greater or lesser reserves being held by the chartered banks or when it buys and sells securities on the market.
All of these actions have a direct effect on the economy as a whole. The philosophy, the policy, ought to be the responsibility of the government and its responsibility alone in precisely the same way as it is now the government's responsibility to make taxation policy. After the minister consults the Governor of the Bank of Canada, consults his deputy, consults his economic advisers and consults, as he did the last time, organizations across the country, he is in the end responsible for taxation policy. In exactly the same way, and indeed a more urgent way, is it necessary that he be responsible for monetary policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Again the hon. gentleman has left out an important step in the process of tax changes. Tax changes come before parliament for approval. He is surely not suggesting that every transaction of the Bank of Canada should be brought to parliament for approval. I do not make the taxation policy. It is this parliament that makes the taxation policy.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, the basic policy of taxation is presented by the minister, and if he is trying to get out of that responsibility in that way let me say to him that there are, I suppose, literally thousands of acts taken in the Department of National Defence, the Department of Public Works and in every other department he can think of based on policies which have an effect on our economy from day to day but which do not come before parliament for our approval. If the monetary policy pursued by the government is wrong in the opinion of parliament there are ways by which we can express criticism such as through motions of non-confidence and so forth, but the fact that the minister takes responsibility does not mean that parliament cannot have its say.
Bank of Canada Act
What I question very seriously is the philosophy behind the proposition that there is something sacrosanct about the Bank of Canada and something sacrosanct about monetary policy that is handed over to people outside the government. The policies followed must be the policies of the minister and the government at all times and under all circumstances, with the Bank of Canada then entrusted to carry them out. My time has expired so I shall resume my seat, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I find the remarks and the general thesis presented by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) most interesting. I agree with the argument he has used with reference specifically to the policy of the Bank of Canada but I agree only up to a point. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), whether or not he will admit it, he has a great deal to do with the actual policy and operations of the Bank of Canada.
At the present time we have a tight money policy in Canada. It is not something new that the amount of money in circulation should be actually used to control deflationary or inflationary tendencies. It is obvious at the present time that the government feels there is a danger of inflation and that it is necessary to institute certain government policies, but I maintain that this is not the policy of the Governor of the Bank of Canada but rather the policy of the government of Canada and that it is merely the governor of the bank who is instituting it.
At the present time we are definitely experiencing a shortage of money for finance and credit and it is a deliberate shortage. It cannot be explained in any way except by the fact that it is a policy of the government and the Minister of Finance. Because the Bank of Canada has as one of its basic functions control over finance and purchasing power in the economy, the Bank of Canada is being used to institute this policy at this time. Whether it is admitted or not, it seems to me that it is at least apparent that the government is making monetary policy and using the Bank of Canada to implement it.
There is nothing wrong with that procedure but I think at this particular time we ought to be concerned with not only the policy but who is actually responsible for that policy so there can be no misunderstanding. In following up the remarks just made by the preceding speaker let me say that this is a

June 13, 1966
Bank of Canada Act
basically important premise which underlies the actual amendments that are being proposed to the Bank of Canada Act.
It was very interesting to hear the minister talk about changing the percentage of reserves so far as banks are concerned in respect of the issuance of credit. When he suggests increasing the amount of reserves under this new formula for adjusting secondary reserves what he is actually doing is putting in words that which is taking place and is the practice at the present time. This can be discussed when we reach our consideration of the bill clause by clause.
So far as monetary policy is concerned it has been the practice during the past number of years to use it as a tool for curbing excessive booms and stimulating lagging economic situations. This is why we now have tight money. The government believes that a tight money policy is the one that should be followed at this time. I am disturbed because bankers, and I am not only referring to private bankers but to Mr. Rasminsky, the present governor, as well, tend to minimize this fact. I do not know why that should be so because I think it is a simple but cold, hard fact. This is surely the reason why we have tight money at the present time. I do not agree with that policy nor with the suggestion that we should be manipulating the actual money supply as it relates to our economy because so long as we can gear the economy to the consumers' needs and their ability to use that which the economy is able to produce I do not think we should be concerned with inflation as such. After all, the only reason why we produce anything is because of the prospect that a consumer somewhere will use it.
The situation at the present time is not inflation in monetary supply but inflation in price. It is through the manipulation of monetary supply that the Minister of Finance is attempting to exercise some control at this time, but it seems to me he is actually doing things in the reverse order. This is not a policy that is new but one that has been considered on several occasions in the past.
I want to remind the Minister of Finance of a speech made by the late prime minister Mackenzie King in 1935 when the Bank of Canada was something new and just being given its present role. At that time he said:
-once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws . . . Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and

recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
On the basis of that statement, which I believe to be correct, there is nothing wrong with the Bank of Canada or the Minister of Finance through his control over the Bank of Canada, being made responsible for the monetary needs of the economy. That is a basic function of government.
In this regard I should like to refer to a statement made by Henry Ford in which he tried to set out this same principle in a practical way. He said:
The function of money is not to make money, but to move goods. Money is only one part of our transportation system. It moves goods from man to man. A dollar bill is like a postage stamp: it is no good unless it will move commodities between persons. If a postage stamp will not carry a letter, or money will not move goods, it is just the same as an engine that will not run. Someone will have to get out and fix it.
Our monetary policy at the present time needs fixing and we should not try to cover up responsibility for the readjustment of monetary policy. That responsibility should be accepted by the Minister of Finance. The policy embodied in the present legislation must fall within the responsibility of the minister and the government. Whether or not they will admit it, that is the fact of the matter.
The Bank of Canada is actually responsible for carrying out the monetary policy of the government in power. Let us face that fact and let us make sure that the policy which is carried out by the Bank of Canada is the policy best suited to the needs of a given economy. We are not simply faced with problems related to automation at this time, we are faced with problems of cybernation. Our problems do not relate only to economic production but to the economy of the consumer, and our monetary policy must be geared to that need. Our problems relate directly to cybernation and all its implications which are fundamentally related to monetary policy and, unless we realize that, a financial breakdown and economic disaster are inevitable. Unless we can implement effective and acceptable means of distributing sufficient purchasing power to consumers, regardless of whether or not they are wage earners, unless we can enable the benefits of total national production to be distributed promptly and efficiently, the economic liberty and freedom of the individual are lost.
June 13, 1966

[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Therefore I suggest to the Minister of Finance that this is his responsibility. Let us make sure that we understand that he as Minister of Finance has laid down a policy so far as the Bank of Canada is concerned which should make effective a monetary policy geared to the consuming needs of our economy, something that is basic at the present time as cybernation takes over more and more.
As we are discussing the principle of this bill I should like to mention a few points in relation to the function of the Bank of Canada which I think substantiate the remarks I have made and are very important as we consider this legislation. The purpose of the Bank of Canada is to control the total money supply of Canada in the best interests of the country, and the most important means of presently accomplishing this is through the sale of government bonds by the Bank of Canada. Actually this makes the Bank of Canada a borrowing agent, an agent in the issuing of government of Canada bonds. In fact, in 1965 the Bank of Canada issued to the market some $1,700 million worth of bonds. In this regard it looked after the preparation, promotion, sale and distribution of these bonds.
Strangely, this year a new policy was instituted which I do not think is a policy of the Governor of the Bank of Canada but is a policy of the Minister of Finance. The Bank of Canada adopted the policy of purchasing some of the bonds it had issued. In fact, at the present time something more than 12 per cent of all the bonds issued by the Bank of Canada have been bought back by the Bank of Canada. It pays itself the interest that is chargeable to these bonds. It comes in as an income to the Bank of Canada and is turned back to the consolidated revenue fund. There is nothing wrong with buying up Canada's debt. It is monetary policy moving in the right direction, but let us face up to it and name it for what it is.
This makes the issuing of the bonds of Canada one of the most important functions of the Bank of Canada and I think it is logical to assume that the government has to take responsibility for this kind of policy. Therefore let us face it. The Bank of Canada also serves as the custodian of these bonds; it even provides the bookkeeping facilities for their sale and transfer. In addition to this service rendered by the Bank of Canada in the issuance of bonds, it is also responsible for getting currency into circulation. In 1965 the
Bank of Canada Act
Bank of Canada printed more than $1,500 million worth of new currency, putting the currency supply at an all-time high of $2,513,600,000. This is a very important function of the Bank of Canada.
In addition the Bank of Canada stores the nation's gold supply, although gold has nothing to do with currency or bonds or with the money that is actually in our pockets. Last year the Bank of Canada stored a basic amount of $1,137 million worth of gold bars in its vaults, allowing for the fluctuation from day to day. But this has nothing to do with the sale of bonds or with the issuance of currency or coinage; it relates only to a reserve for foreign exchange. These are the basic functions of the Bank of Canada. I am not trying to oversimplify them but am relating them specifically to the responsibility of seeing that the economy of Canada has an adequate amount of purchasing power in the form of money.
This being so, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the policy which governs the Bank of Canada is very basic and fundamental. This responsibility cannot just be passed over to the one responsible for the administration of that policy, the management of the Bank of Canada. It comes right back to the government, and this legislation is very basically related to it.
In our economy at the present time I think some obvious things are not being considered in the drafting of policy as it relates to the Bank of Canada. No longer is it adequate that we merely classify capital in two groups, tax capital which is collected from the pockets of the taxpayers to pay for the services rendered by government, and private capital in the private enterprise system under which we operate. The tremendous need for capital for development in the public sector requires recognition of a third classification of capital, namely, public or social capital. This is the kind of money that is needed to build our schools, hospitals, harbours, bridges, highways, projects which in themselves do not earn money but merely facilitate a service, projects which are liquidated over a period of years of amortization.
Unless we make provision within our monetary policy for the recognition of this additional type of capital we are going to be faced with a constant increase in the cost of servicing our national debt, a constant increase in the debt and taxation structure of the country. As long ago as 1963 the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities submitted

June 13, 1966
Bank of Canada Act
a brief to the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance. Their main recommendation was:
That the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, should establish a national municipal loan fund (or bank) for the purpose of facilitating the borrowing operations of municipal governments.
I mention this because the most acute and difficult area of governmental finance today is not at the federal or provincial but at the municipal level, because the amount of municipal debt increases year by year. It is interesting to note that the municipal bonded debt in Canada rose from $833 million in 1946 to nearly $9 billion in 1965. This is an increase of approximately 10 times in 20 years.
Together with this increase in municipal bonded debt has come a tremendous increase in the cost of servicing the debt. This is illustrated on the federal scene as well because at the present time more than $1,180 million of tax dollars is used to service the national debt of this country. I maintain that if the government would recognize the need of adding to its monetary policy the recognition of a third sector of capital, the public sector, whether it be called public capital or social capital, we would not be faced with the difficulties in regard to monetary policy that we face at the present time which the government is trying to control the economy with a tight money policy resulting in the amount of money in circulation actually being decreased. This is the type of manipulation which is being used by the government as a means of control and for which the Minister of Finance must take responsibility. This policy does not work in the best interests of the economy because we see what is happening at the present time. We are not building the number of houses that we should build. Goods are not moving because there is not the money in circulation. Those things which we recognize as being desirable objectives in our economy are not being attained because of the policies of the government.
Our monetary policy is restrictive in this regard. The United States market this year is already approximately three times greater than it was last year. The policies of this government are defeating what should be the purpose of our monetary policy. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, unless the government and the Minister of Finance assume their responsibility and recognize the fact that the Bank of Canada is merely the means of carrying out policy, we will go along from boom to bust,

from depression to prosperity, from inflation to deflation with a constant increase in the cost of living and the cost of taxes. In addition, the higher the cost of living goes the more strikes we will have such as the ones we are faced with today which seriously affect our economy. We are also not giving any consideration to those on fixed incomes, particularly those living on pensions which were fixed at a time when the cost of living was not nearly as high, and the whole economy and the Canadian people generally suffer as a result.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
So, Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Finance had better face up to the fact that he is responsible for the policy of the Bank of Canada and that only if that policy is adjusted to the needs of the economy are we ever going to have a satisfactory monetary policy. I suggest that the federal government use the Bank of Canada to provide capital-I am speaking now of the third category, public capital-free of interest for every construction loan necessary to finance national capital wealth projects such as the seaway and other internal waterways, hospital facilities, tourist attractions, schools or any other type of project for which the government has to borrow money. We cannot find reserves of capital in Canada under the present tight money policy, so we go to the United States, borrow money there and place ourselves in bondage which we agree is not in the best national interest.
If the Bank of Canada can print the bonds of Canada, if it can be responsible for the currency needs of this country, why can it not be responsible for this kind of credit as well? This newly created real wealth would balance out with the newly created financial grants needed to produce it. If we did that we could let the international exchange rate float. This would then supply the additional Canadian capital so badly needed. Therefore, if monetary policy is to be realistic so far as the present situation is concerned the Bank of Canada should be authorized to form what might be called a municipal development bank, in the same way as the Industrial Development Bank is a division of the Bank of Canada, to provide the public or social capital that this economy needs. This would obviate the necessity for the present tight money policy because adequate money would be provided to the private sector for the development of our commerce and industry. I think that the Bank of Canada is basically
June 13, 1966

responsible for the administration of this kind of policy but it is the government which is responsible for its institution.
Therefore, in closing, I wish to make this suggestion to the Minister of Finance. In view of the fact that apparently he does not wish to admit responsibility for the monetary policy of this country but would sooner pass it on to the Governor of the Bank of Canada and in view of the argument he put to the previous speaker in regard to this very subject, I suggest to him that if he wishes to attune our monetary policy to the needs of our economy he should create a permanent monetary commission. We in the Social Credit party have advocated this for as long as 20 years. This commission would be responsible for the determination and spelling out of the monetary policy as put forward by the Minister of Finance to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Representatives from the Bank of Canada, from the chartered banks, the Department of Finance, agriculture, labour and business throughout the country should sit on this commission. The commission might perhaps be an expansion of the board of the Bank of Canada and would meet regularly to consider all questions with regard to the financial and monetary policy of the country.
In our view such a permanent monetary commission could be made directly responsible to the representatives of the people in the House of Commons in the same way as the Auditor General is responsible. It could be called periodically before the appropriate committee of the House of Commons to give an account before the members of this house of what is the actual monetary policy of this country instead of it being kicked back and forth between the political side and the Bank of Canada. I believe this would provide for a much more satisfactory monetary policy, the implementation of which is the responsibility of the Bank of Canada.
I will end my statement at this point because we must get into committee so we can have a full discussion of Bill C-190. Regardless of whether or not the Minister of Finance is willing to listen to the suggestions I have made, I believe he will have to admit that under the present set-up he is responsible for the final, fiscal policy of this government. We need something more adequate than the tight money policy which the government is apparently favouring at present because it is defeating the very purpose of the Bank of Canada which is to make sure
Bank of Canada Act
that an adequate monetary supply is provided to the economy of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise and, as a pragmatic socialist, support wholeheartedly the ideas put forward by the member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). I have never understood why our provinces and municipalities have had to go to the New York money market to borrow money when this credit would be issued on the basis of Canadian national resources, Canadian industrial equipment and the ability of Canadians to produce. I support wholeheartedly his contention that this is a function which should be performed at cost by the Bank of Canada for the Canadian people. I agree with him that such a monetary policy would enable us to retain control of our economy and to obtain the social and private capital that is required for the development of our country. This is a mystery to me which I have never been able to understand.
In this connection I wish to quote from one or two letters. I have here a letter from the Department of Finance dated May 21, 1952, which reads as follows:
Dear Sir,
I have your letter of May 6, 1952, and am replying to your questions in the order in which you ask them.
1.	The Bank of Canada holds many securities in its investment portfolio which form part of the unmatured funded debt but its weekly statement does not show a breakdown of its holdings by issues. At the time of issue the bank may purchase small securities both for its clients (other government agencies) and for itself, but the relative amounts are not disclosed.
2.	As and when securities are issued to the Bank of Canada, payment is made by a deposit to the credit of the Receiver General's account with the
bank.
3.	You will notice on page 54 of the 1951 public accounts that the summary of security issues and redemptions during the year specifically excludes treasury bills. Treasury bills included in "unmatured funded debt" are not shown in the table of new security issues for reasons of space. They are issued on the average every second week and including them in the table of new security issues would mean a listing of about 24 items.
Treasury bills appear in appendix No. 7, pages 112 to 113 of the 1950-51 public accounts about the middle of the page. They are shown as having paid interest varying in rate from .512 per cent to .755 per cent.
4.	$200 million treasury notes were originally issued on May 1, 1947 to provide funds for the redemption of various refunding loans.

June 13, 1966
Bank of Canada Act
Why could this not be done at the present time?
$550 million treasury notes were issued on March 1, 1947 to replace a substantial part of $606 million treasury notes issued on September 1, 1946.
This gentleman, who is a very important member of the Department of Finance, goes on to say:
$90 million 1.5 per cent bonds issued on November 1, 1949 and due November 1, 1952 was part of a total of $300 million issued in connection with the redemption of $268 million 1 per cent 8th Victory Loan issued on May 1, 1945 to the public for cash and the $290 million 4.5 per cent conversion loan issued on May 1, 1931 and called for payment on November 1, 1949.
$185,495,000 1.5 per cent bonds due March 1, 1953 was part of a total of $325 million issued as a renewal of 1.5 per cent bonds due March 1, 1950, which bonds were issued on March 1, 1948 for cash.
[DOT] (7:50 pm.)
5.	As you will have gathered from the above, the three year bonds with maturities on November 1. 1952 and March 1, 1953 are shown in the total, namely, $300,000,000 and $325,000,000 respectively, in Appendix No. 5, page 108 of the 1950-51 public accounts.
6.	During the fiscal years ended March 31, 1951 and 1952 redemption of securities issued to the Bank of Canada totalled $1,500,000,000 represented by four issues of six-month treasury notes. Funds for the redemption of these notes were provided by the issue of new notes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very clear.

Yes.
7.	Various expenditures listed under the heading of War Demobilization and Reconversion, Special Expenditures and Government-Owned Enterprises have no corresponding assets in the accounts of Canada. There are no itemized statistics available showing the classes and amounts of such expenditures, short of tracing such expenditures through public accounts for the various years.
The government's practice in recording assets and liabilities was explained by the then minster of finance in his budget speech of May 18, 1920, when he said, in part, "Assets which are not readily convertible, as the specie reserve is convertible, or are not interest producing, are not such assets as ought to be deducted from the gross debt".
Appendix 27 of the public accounts for 1938, shows the adjustments authorized by the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act, 1937.
Yours very truly,
W. C. Clark
I have read that, Mr. Speaker, to indicate what is possible if the Bank of Canada were only used for the Canadian people as a whole. I should like to make reference to a bill, No. 297, to amend the Bank of Canada Act which received first reading on February 22, 1954. It was piloted by the then minister of finance. Section 18 (1) (c) of the bill read:
Buy or sell securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province.

This was the explanatory note:
Paragraph (c) of subsection (1) removes the limitation imposed by former paragraph (d) of subsection (1).
Paragraph (d), which was repealed, read:
Buy and sell securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province having a maturity exceeding two years from the date of acquisition by the bank, but the bank shall at no time hold securities not maturing within two years having a par value in excess of 50 per cent of its outstanding note issue and deposit liabilities, nor shall the bank at any time hold securities not maturing within ten years of a par value in excess of five times the amount of the paid-up capital and rest fund of the bank.
Before I conclude I should like to quote part of a letter written by Mr. K. W. Taylor, former deputy minister of finance, dated July 26, 1957. He said:
You are correct in your assumption that the Bank of Canada pays for its purchases of bills by crediting the purchase price to the account of the Receiver General of Canada with the Bank of Canada.
I have quoted the correspondence from Mr. Clark and Mr. Taylor, former deputy ministers of finance, to indicate the capacity of the Bank of Canada to provide social and private capital for the development of this country.
As a pragmatic socialist I wholeheartedly support the arguments which were put forward by the hon. member for Red Deer for the utilization of the Bank of Canada for the issuance of loans to provinces and municipalities on the basis of the security they can advance in terms of natural resources, industrial equipment and the capacity of the Canadian people to produce so that they will not have to continue to go cap in hand to New York for money. This would be entirely unnecessary if we used our own Bank of Canada properly.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs.

Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Fund Act and the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this statute adjustment bill, which is a bill of the type very often urged on us by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). The hon. member has said that we should not run these items through the estimates but rather should have a statutory adjustment bill, and this is what we now have in front of us.
As I indicated when speaking on the resolution which preceded first reading of this bill, the main purpose of this legislation is to provide for the co-ordination of a number of acts dealing with the provision of superannuation benefits for members of the public service of Canada with the Canada Pension Plan, as well as the Quebec Pension Plan in the case of persons employed in the province of Quebec.
The acts which are to be co-ordinated in a variety of ways that will be explained in the course of the debate are the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act and the Intercolonial Prince Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Fund Act. The references to the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act and the Canadian Corporation for the 1967 World Exhibition Act appear in the title of the bill for reasons unconnected with the Canada Pension Plan legislation.
Hon. members will by now have had an opportunity to study the various methods by which it is proposed to accomplish co-ordination of the various measures I have mentioned and at the same time satisfy the principles which were explained at the resolution stage.
I should like to state again that the first principle that the total contributions paid by the employee and by the government on a salary on which contributions are now being paid under the relevant superannuation acts should not be increased. In order to accomplish this a portion of the contributions has to be diverted away from the superannuation fund to the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan, as the case may be.
For example, for male contributors to the public service superannuation plan the reduction will be from 6.5 to 4.7 per cent in respect of that portion of salary from $600 to
Pensions
$5,000 which is subject to Canada Pension Plan contributions. For female contributors it will be from 5 per cent to 3.2 per cent in respect of that same salary portion.
While the percentage figure may differ for other increments, the amount of existing contribution rates which is to be diverted to the Canada Pension Plan or Quebec Pension Plan, as the case may be, will be the same, 1.8 per cent from $600 to $5,000 in every instance.
Reduction in the rates of contributions payable to the various superannuation funds means that the benefits payable out of these funds will likewise have to be reduced in respect of the period of service beginning January 1, 1966 for which the lower contributions will be made. In giving effect to this reduction the second principle comes into play, namely, that the combination of benefits under the relevant superannuation acts and the Canada Pension Plan after the reduction takes place should not be less than the benefits which would have been payable under the formula in the relevant superannuation acts prior to these amendments.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
These proposals do not affect in any way the entitlement of persons who retired prior to the coming into effect of the Canada Pension Plan. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the intention of this plan is to affect contributions and benefits of members of the civil service of Canada or the public service of Canada subsequent to the present date. Consequently persons who have already retired prior to January 1, 1966, need have no concern that their benefits will be reduced because of the advent of the Canada Pension Plan. It is just not possible for this to happen under the provisions of this particular act, or that any portion of the contributions which they have made prior to January 1, 1966 will be transferred to the Canada Pension Plan account.
It was not long after the Canada Pension Plan was announced that requests for the adoption of the two principles I have mentioned were made to the government. These requests came from the staff associations themselves. In response to these requests the Minister of Finance referred to his advisory committee on the Public Service Superannuation Act the question of developing a formula which would meet these requirements in so far as that act was concerned. The advisory committee, which is made up of

portion of their combined benefits is concerned, from the escalation provisions contained in that legislation.
Hon. members will be interested to note that 95 per cent of the members of the regular forces and 80 per cent of the members of the R.C.M.P. will fall within the scope of the integration provisions which I have described. Fewer than 5 per cent of the members of the armed forces, those who enrolled prior to 1939, and fewer than 20 per cent of the members of the R.C.M.P. come within the scope of the continuation acts which I have mentioned and are thereby excluded from both the contribution requirements and the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan.
The next area of general interest which I should like to mention is the one which provides for greater portability of pension benefits. Perhaps the most important of these is the new clause in the Public Service Superannuation Act which would extend the power of the minister-and here I mean the Minister of Finance-to enter into reciprocal pension transfer agreements with any employer with an approved pension plan. This, in practice, means a plan of a type which is acceptable for income tax deduction purposes. A further provision extends the provision in the existing law under which actuarial equivalent benefits may be payable prior to the age of 60 under the Public Service Superannuation Act, while other clauses would permit the compulsory locking-in of contributions made after a date to be proclaimed by the governer in council in the case of a person retiring after the age of 45 with at least ten years of service. Most if not all of these changes are being introduced for the purpose of achieving a greater increase of portability in relation to other employer-employee pension plans in Canada.
It is the introduction of this concept of portability of pensions which is responsible for many of the amendments in the Diplomatic Service (Special) Superannuation Act where, as a result, benefits will henceforth become payable as a matter of right instead of being subject to a grant by the governor in council.
Still other clauses in the bill are designed to broaden the categories of employees covered by the Public Service Superannuation Act. Prevailing rate and seasonal employees will now be required to become contributors at an earlier date than has heretofore been the case. As a result they will derive the
Pensions
added advantage that they will be covered by the supplementary death benefit plan under part II of the Public Service Superannuation Act as well.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The bill provides for the removal of the present ceiling of $5,000 on the death benefit. In its place will be a provision setting the amount of death benefit at the multiple of $250 equal to or next above the salary of the employee. Actuarial advice indicates that this feature can be added to the plan for civil servants without jeopardizing the soundness of the plan. Rates for the civil servants who are covered will remain unchanged at 10 cents for every $250 of coverage.
Members of the regular forces have also been included under this plan and will be eligible, like members of the civil service, for the larger amounts of benefit. Their experience, however, as a younger and healthier group has been so much more favourable than that of civil servants that the adoption of this provision for a higher ceiling, related in the same way to their pay, can be accompanied by a reduction in the rate of contribution from 10 cents to 5 cents a month for every $250 of coverage. Since this would create a basic difference between the two groups of participants under Part II of the Public Service Superannuation Act and could create some confusion in the future, it is proposed to drop the members of the regular forces from this part of the Public Service Superannuation Act and to add a new Part III instead to the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act to provide them with coverage.
Basically this means that members of the armed forces will receive a higher death benefit at a much lower cost and rather than tie this in with the present superannuation act we shall create a new Part III in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act. In effect, members of the forces will be able to get $1,000 coverage for 20 cents a month.
Hon. members will have noted that the bill seeks to remove a number of anomalies which have become evidence in the administration of the acts during the years since they came into force or were last amended. I do not propose to deal with most of these at the present time but will be pleased to explain the remedial provisions on reaching the various clauses concerned at the committee stage should any questions be asked.
Three or four amendments are proposed to give recognition to recommendations of the

public accounts committee while others are of a purely administrative nature to deal with changes which appear necessary as a result of the experience gained over the years. In other words, where we have been introducing $1 items to carry many of the necessary changes in this particular legislation over the years we are now, following the recommendation of the hon. member for Carleton, introducing a statute amendment act to take care of these necessary amendments.
In keeping with the objective of giving more of the detailed administrative responsibility to the department administering the acts, there are a number of amendments which transfer certain authority from the Treasury Board to the appropriate minister.
In so far as the handling of the superannuation account is concerned, the three main superannuation acts, those dealing with the public service, the armed forces and the R.C.M.P., are being amended to implement the government's proposal for the systematic amortization of any deficits which arise from salary revisions or are reported as a result of the statutory quinquennial actuarial reviews of the superannuation accounts established under those acts. This complex problem is referred to in the Auditor-General's report for the year ended March 31, 1965, pages 34-37, as well as in previous years' reports. Following a policy statement on this matter by the former minster of finance on March 6, 1964, legislation was approved by parliament and given royal assent on June 2, 1965, for the purpose of ensuring that actuarial deficits in any of the main superannuation accounts arising from salary revisions affecting a significant number of public servants would be amortized on a systematic basis by equal contributions over a five-year period.
In this respect I should like to compliment the former minister of finance for what he did in this regard and draw attention to what the previous government failed to do by way of providing actuarial requirements of the superannuation account. Instead hon. gentlemen opposite let it grow into the huge deficit which faced this government when it took office.

The wording of the superannuation legislation permits days of authorized absence from employment to be counted for pension purposes under conditions which are spelled out in the act and regulations but does not provide for the counting of days of unauthorized absence. When this problem came to the attention of the responsible officials last December it was decided that legislative authority would be sought at the earliest possible opportunity to permit coverage of all postal employees for the days in question, even though these were days when the majority of postal workers were engaged in an unauthorized work stoppage. One of the amendments proposed in this present bill will give the governor in council authority to deal with this particular and, I hope, isolated problem by special regulation. I am sure that under the new collective bargaining legislation, to be reviewed by the committee which has been established for this purpose, this sort of thing will not happen again in the future.
I am satisfied that the provisions I have described will go far to meet the problems which have been the subject of representations by many retired members of the armed forces and by members on the other side of this house. The government, if given the authority to deal with this problem by regulation, will continue to keep the matter under periodic review and take such further action as subsequent experience with the proposed new regulations indicates to be desirable. Mr. Speaker, if there be a more complex and complicated bill to come before parliament this session, I hope someone other than myself may be its critic. To work one's way through the intricate labyrinth of the diverse provisions of this bill is a task for a Philadelphia lawyer and I do not think an Ottawa solicitor or a Kingston accountant has achieved that particular distinction.

I am sure the hon. gentleman is going to have many questions to answer in committee stage, and I hope it is going to be at committee stage in a special joint committee and not in committee of the whole.
I say that none but an actuarial expert could be certain that he fully understands the technical and involved draftsmanship of this bill. It is for that reason I submit it is imperative that the bill should be sent to the special joint committee on the public service rather than to have it considered in the first instance by the committee of the whole. I appeal to the minister to adopt this suggestion because I am certain it will save time in the long run.
In all candour I say to the minister that I have tried as earnestly and valiantly as I can to study this bill in great detail and to seek to understand the integration of the proposed amendments with the existing superannuation structure. As a result I wish I could assert that I had made myself the master of the amendments. I have not, and when a member who has the background which I have in superannuation problems, from professional practice in the city of Ottawa over the years, from service in the last parliamentary committee on superannuation, and from extensive handling of superannuation matters as parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance, when such a member is perplexed

about this bill I am sure there are other members equally perplexed, perhaps even the minister himself, for I thought that in his statement tonight he demonstrated that perplexity.
Before that special joint committee we would have the opportunity to examine experts, particularly that knowledgeable, yes, that brilliant pension expert, Mr. Hart D. Clark, to hear representatives of the staff associations and to assure ourselves that this bill is a wise and proper revision of the superannuation provisions.
There are three other reasons why I submit this bill should go to the special joint committee. First, I have reason to believe, as has the minister, that the staff associations have not yet had the opportunity to study the bill. I believe the minister has had a telegram from at least one staff association, and perhaps two, objecting to the consideration, so early in the proceedings of this house, of this bill. This bill has been available for only six days and I believe it would be offensive to the staff associations, and indeed court real trouble, to proceed with a bill which so intimately affects every civil servant until the representative staff associations have had a proper opportunity to study it and to make representations.
I shall be frank with the minister and say to him that if he persists in ramming this bill into committee of the whole, clause 2 will not be passed until we on this side are given assurances by staff associations that they have had the opportunity to examine the bill in detail and have no objection to it, or have such objection as may be stated and then debated. I am most anxious to be co-operative with the minister but I am equally determined that the civil service shall be protected and the staff associations shall have the opportunity to examine the bill and to say whether it is satisfactory to their members.
Second, sir, I think it is quite evident that if the special joint committee does not examine the bill the Senate will send the bill to one of its committees. I do not believe that we who represent the public service of Canada in this elected chamber should abdicate our rights to the other place.
Third, the special joint committee could divide this bill into seven components and report seven bills to the house rather than this single, omnibus bill. I repeat what I said at resolution stage, that this technique of

legislating by omnibus bill is sloppy, confusing and untidy, and I say it is genuine legislative heresy. I really thought it was quite cute of the minister to try to attribute to me the authorship of this particular type of legislation.
Yes, I did say on the estimates and I will repeat on the estimates that, instead of having dollar items, for those simple and ordinary situations which are not matters of principle there should be a statute law amendment act. I never said, and the minister cannot find it said in any place by me, that matters of principle should be legislated in an omnibus bill, and I say to him tonight that that is evil per se. I say this house ought not to permit what is being done in this bill. This issue was argued on the government's reorganization bill and I adopt all the arguments then advanced.
If the government is permitted to get away with this new legislative technique of amending seven bills by a single bill, it will not be long until the whole governmental legislative program is contained in each session in one single bill. I repeat that this legislative omnibus practice is evil per se and the time to stop it is now on this bill.
I think the minister is one of the more reasonable of the present ministry. I appeal to him to accept these arguments and to send the bill to the special joint committee. If he does not agree there will be a time when we shall have to test the sense of the house in this particular.
The integration of the Canada Pension Plan and the various superannuation acts has been a difficult and complex task. It is something that ought to have been done long ago. It ought to have been done at the time the Canada Pension Plan was brought forward. We are now suffering from the neglect at that particular time.
All of us will need to study carefully what the minister said tonight before we can approve or disapprove of the proposals he has made. What he has said has been technical in every detail. Surely, sir, since he has announced tonight some of these procedures and techniques for the first time, he cannot object legitimately to an opportunity for members of the opposition and officials of the staff associations to study his statement, and I think I must insist upon that opportunity before this bill proceeds further.
There are some features of the bill of which I approve fully. For example, the inclusion of wartime service as the equivalent
[Mr. Bell (Carleton) .1
of service in the regular forces removes an anomoly which should never have been permitted to arise. It will bring justice to a considerable number of officers and men now approaching retirement age.
The intention to take authority to modify the existing harsh provisions relating to pensioned officers of the armed forces who enter the public service is a step forward. What happened tonight is that the minister obviously had two or three pages of his notes in which he meant to describe to us precisely what was intended by this. He skipped those pages and jumped to the end, saying he was sure the house would agree with what he had just described.
Although he gave us a commitment, positive and clear, at the time of the resolution stage that he would describe all these matters on second reading he has not done so tonight. He has again postponed the situation and said he will do it when we are in committee of the whole. I think the minister at the resolution stage was less generous and less graceful than he usually is when he refused to satisfy our curiosity in relation to these matters, but his failure tonight to give an outline of what is proposed is intolerable.
What he is asking for is a blank cheque, and if an additional reason be required for this bill to go to a special joint committee then I say this is it. Clause 2 certainly should not be passed until the representatives of the armed forces have had an opportunity to express their opinion on proposals which the minister has yet failed to outline to the house despite his specific commitment to that effect. Certainly, sir, I would prefer, whatever the proposals of the government may be in this respect, that they should be part of the bill and not included in an authority to enact regulations, which is the purpose of the present proposal.
I am opposed to giving blank cheques to anyone, but this is what we are being asked to sign for the minister. I oppose this bypassing of parliament in respect of this particular situation. It is all very well for the minister to assert that under the R.C.M.P. legislation, enacted when the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert was prime minister, there was an equivalent provision.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Perhaps we did make a mistake at that time. We were not infallible, but I have no patience with these tu quoque arguments. This parliament has suffered too much from this "you're another" approach, "tit for tat", a

*"Roland for an Oliver", and other forms of argument of this sort. All I wish to know is what is right in the existing circumstances, and I doubt if this can be ascertained without hearing evidence before a joint committee. I know this cannot be permitted to pass when the minister only explains what his proposals are when we come to our consideration of the particular clauses of the legislation. There must be an opportunity for a representative of the armed forces to know what is intended before we come to that, and to know what is proposed by the government.
One aspect of the delegated authority to make regulations is that the pensioned armed forces officers, warrant officers or petty officers, who are afterwards employed by an agent of Her Majesty, may have their pensions placed in jeopardy. This has not been the case in the past when a retired officer was employed by a crown corporation. Although this	has	been the	case with theR.C.M.P. in the past it is now imported into armed forces provisions for the first time. Obviously I agree that the treatment should be uniform,	but	it	should	be generous. Irepeat, sir, that I have the gravest reservations about	what	is	proposed in this particular and	I must	insist	that before we
advance at all in this legislation the minister tell this house what he intends.
One feature of the bill, which runs through many clauses, vests in a single minister powers heretofore exercised only by the Treasury Board. As emphatically as I can I oppose this proposal. No doubt the draftsman of this bill thought it would be neat and tidy, and in theory that is correct. But political practicalities are not always neat and tidy. The futures of many individuals are being delivered into the decision of a single minister. I have a very vivid recollection of how harassed a minister may be at a particular time and how he will sign, however strong-minded he may be, the documents put before him by trusted advisers just merely to end the horrible day. If the documents he signs are only recommendations to the Treasury Board two checks ensue, first, a careful scrutiny by the Treasury Board staff and, second, a review by at least three ministers on Treasury Board. One may argue whether three harassed ministers are better than one, but at least mistakes may be caught. The mere fact of Treasury Board review is a salutary deterrent to arbitrariness at the departmental level.
I ask the minister to consider this point of view. I do not seek to move amendments to
Pensions
each of the many clauses which, for purposes obviously of so-called administrative convenience, seek to vest in a single minister authority heretofore exercised by Treasury Board, but will the minister consider that there is a check and a balance in multiplicity of review? If he does not concede that, will he consider whether some appellate procedure is required? I will return to this subject during our committee consideration.
May I now turn to the question of the actuarial status of the superannuation funds. The new bill will provide for the immediate crediting to the superannuation acts of the amounts necessary to provide increased benefits as the result of salary increases and would spread payment of that amount over five equal annual instalments. I venture to draw specific attention to the reply I received to a question which appears in Hansard, for Monday, June 6, at page 5980. The position may actually be summarized by the answer to part 4 of that question, the question being:
4. What is the total actuarial deficiency in the public service superannuation accounts as of March 31, 1966, for which no provision has been charged to budgetary expenditure?
The answer was:
4. Public service superannuation account, $93,620,600; Canadian forces superannuation account, $53,601,200; Royal Canadian Mounted Police superannuation account, $3,115,200.
In other words, among the three funds there is an actuarial deficiency for which no provision has been charged to budgetary expenditures of over $150 million.

It is all very well to spread this over a period of years but if the impact is that it becomes larger year by year then this is a matter that must be considered by parliament.
I want to say to the minister that this bill is actually much more significant in its omissions than in its provisions, and I refer basically to four principles upon which the bill improperly is either silent or less explicit than it should be.
First, the vaunted provisions of the bill allegedly providing for portability, and the minister spoke tonight about this at some length, are much less than satisfactory. Indeed, all of us would agree that mobility of manpower is one of the most significant requirements for these days of advancing automation. The government of Canada should set the standard for all employers and should make full portability possible. The provisions of this bill instead are trivial and insignificant in this field. A genuine national plan of portability of private pensions is an urgent need and the government should set the model. It should start to set the model by this bill dealing with its own employees and should then set a model in a bill which deals with portability for those employees who are under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, which would integrate other bills which I hope could be passed by all legislatures of the provinces. There is opportunity here for this parliament to give the lead in portability of pensions.
Second, I submit that all superannuation acts dealt with by this bill should now have a built-in escalation clause which would reflect rising costs and changes in salary scales. Under the Canada Pension Plan a technique of escalation of benefits has been adopted. This has been accepted as a matter of government policy for all Canadians. I submit it should be introduced into the various superannuation acts for the public service as a technique of avoiding the hardships and injustices which are bound to confront many present civil servants when they retire, as they have confronted so many civil servants

already retired. These hardships and injustices are the result of the lack of an escalation clause. An escalation clause in the public service superannuation and associated acts would have a further salutary advantage in that it might set a significant standard for industry generally.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Third, I submit that this bill ought to provide for a reduction to a five-year average instead of the present six-year average. This would have a further advantage in bringing pensions more in line with current conditions. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in office years ago they raised it from a five-year average to a ten-year average. When the government of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert was in office it was reduced from ten to six. I think now it ought to be brought down to a five-year average and ought to reflect, as a five-year average would, a closer approach to what are the economic conditions at the time of retirement.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, this bill perpetuates the existing shabby and shoddy treatment of retired civil servants, retired members of the R.C.M.P. and of the armed forces. Persistently before 1957 and since 1963, hon. gentlemen opposite have scorned the claims of retired civil servants consonant with the erosion of the value of their pensions due to the fall in the value of money.

Mr. Speaker, my interest in this bill is in the main twofold. On the one hand I am interested in it from the point of view of parliament's responsibility to our public servants. I want to see a piece of legislation that deals with their pension rights in the fairest possible way. On the other hand I am interested in this bill in so far as it sets a pattern with respect to the integration of other pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan. Because it does set a pattern, it may well be followed or used as an excuse by private
June 13. 1966

employers. I feel therefore that we have to look at this piece of legislation very carefully before we give it final approval.
I therefore share the desire of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) that this bill be looked at in the best possible way. He has suggested that it should be referred after second reading to the special joint committee on the public service and I think that that proposal has much to commend it. I recognize the problem that exists because three other heavy pieces of legislation have been referred to that committee and if we have four bills of the weight of these pieces of legislation the committee may find itself in session until Christmas.
Nevertheless I hope that the minister and the government will find some way to meet the point that the member for Carleton has raised. I do not know whether there is any rule under which we could refer a bill to a committee for a short period of time. That might be one answer to the problem. Another way might be to refer this bill to a special committee consisting of the limited number of members of this house who have studied it so that the civil servants who have drafted it for us might be able to give us the benefit of their knowledge of this legislation.
1 think that one of the most useful aspects of the experience which we had as members of the special joint committee on the Canada Pension Plan was that we had before that committee civil servants who took us through the bill clause by clause and enabled us to understand it in all of its detail. I think that is needed with respect to this bill. It is so complicated that I do not suppose every member of the house would want to know the meaning of every section but I think that at least a representative number of members of the House of Commons should know pretty clearly what is contained in this legislation and some vehicle should be found whereby we can deal with it more effectively than will be the case in the committee of the whole house.
I am putting forward these thoughts not in the spirit of any threat nor in an argumentative manner but rather in the belief that this bill deserves better consideration than it will get if we deal with it in committee of the whole house. After all, it contains 94 clauses and it comprises 72 pages. It is not much shorter than the Canada Pension Plan itself. The details of this bill are complex and it excels most bills in the way in which it can reduce mathematical formulae to many para-
Pensions
graphs of words. It seems to me to give a different treatment to the same subject matter under the different acts with which we are dealing. For these reasons it is the complex piece of legislation described by the previous speaker.
I hope, therefore, that the government will discuss with hon. members representing the various parties the possibility of finding some way in which we can study this bill more thoroughly and more effectively than we can in committee of the whole. If that is what we have to do, some of us are ready to do it but I think the bill deserves better than that.
