I have two other suggestions which I should like to make. One is that I think at some point the government should produce what we call a white paper on these various pension plans. Perhaps this is something that does not need to be done until after the legislation has been passed. But just as it was necessary to produce a white paper on the Canada Pension Plan so that the public could understand that piece of legislation, I think the same will have to be done with respect to the Public Service Superannuation Act as it is affected by this bill, the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act as it is affected by this bill, and so on with all the other pieces of legislation. After all, the number of people affected by these various government pension plans adds up to a considerable section of what we call the public, and I think that they have the right to a white paper, or to a document, call it what you may, in which they can read in understandable language what are the provisions of their pension plans and what are their rights under those plans.
The other suggestion which I think may be appropriate, having spent a good portion of the week end wading through Bill No. C-193, is that perhaps we need another Carter Commission. Perhaps I should withhold the use of that name until we have seen what the Carter Commission produces by way of a report; but in so far as we have any notion of what the Carter Commission is supposed to do, we understand that it is supposed to take a look at the complexities of our income tax structure to see whether or not there are ways in which they can be simplified. I suggest that the time has arrived when it may be necessary to simplify to some extent the complexities of our many pension plans, particularly those which come under government supervision.

I know why these plans as they now stand are so complex: they were drafted in the first instance; then proposals were made for changes and amendments; and then as amendments were added certain qualifications had to be recognized. And so on the story goes; and while the plan did not grow just like Topsy, it did grow in all sorts of directions and, as I say, we now have a very complex system of pension plans.
Therefore, I believe that consideration may have to be given to the establishment of something like the Carter Royal Commission to see whether it is possible to simplify these plans and to put them on a more readily understandable basis. It may be, or course, that the idea of a commission to survey all our pension plans could wait for a few years until the Canada Pension Plan comes into full operation and until other plans have established their relationships with it. When that time comes such a commission would find that it would have to go not only into government pension plans but into all pension plans in this country; and I think that day is coming soon. Pensions are becoming a very important aspect of our economy, and as they become important and as the capacity to enjoy retirement with a decent standard of living becomes recognized, I suggest it also becomes urgent that our whole pensions structure be looked at and made as simple and as understandable as possible, in view of the right of those affected to know what is in these plans.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to a few comments on bill No. C-193 itself, and I use the word "few" advisedly because with a bill consisting of 94 clauses one does not go into all the points on second reading but leaves something for whatever stage we are going to have later. The first thing I want to say is that as I read the bill it does come through with the things that the government said it would do in this legislation. Some of those things which it said it would do are details of which we approve, such as bringing in the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, establishing portability, taking care of the post office workers who were out on strike last summer and so on. But, of course, the main purpose of the bill was to establish a basis for integration of the various government pension plans with the Canada Pension Plan, and this the bill does.
Furthermore, this integration is accomplished in line with the original statement that was made on the matter on behalf of

the government as recorded in Hansard for November 18, 1964, at pages 10233 to 10235. The member who made that statement was the then parliamentary secretary to the minister of finance, now the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell). That was the first official statement on what the government had in mind regarding the integration of these various employee plans with the Canada Pension Plan and, as I say, the bill before us carries out what the present Solicitor General indicated on that occasion.
I suppose that because I stand here and say that the bill does what the government said it would do, this should be taken as a compliment and nothing more need be said. However, I find I must repeat the statement which I have made on previous occasions, namely, that I am not yet sold on the principle of as complete an integration of other plans with the Canada Pension Plan as that proposed by the government in this legislation.
I shall come in a moment or two to the question of the extent to which there is complete integration as opposed to the extent to which integration is but partial, but in the main this bill is a piece of legislation the effect of which is to deny to civil servants either all or part of the extra benefit which they might have received had the Canada Pension Plan been recognized simply as a supplement or addition to what they already have.
I know all of the arguments about the public service superannuation plan being a good one and about its rates of contribution being high, but it still seems to me that an arrangement could have been made to enable public servants to get a better share of the extra benefit which is available to Canadians because of the Canada Pension Plan.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, when we were at the resolution stage I believed, and I still believe, that the purpose of the Canada Pension Plan was to provide a pension for employees who did not already have one. Its purpose also was to provide an additional pension for those already had some pension rights and benefits. I feel very sad when I see any group of workers or employees denied the possible chance of an improved pension such as the Canada Pension Plan was designed to provide.

Let me document what I mean about the denial of the extra benefits of the Canada Pension Plan to the public servants. The formula as worked out in the bill, when it gets into language, is pretty complicated. But when one reduces it to mathematical characters it is not quite so difficult to understand. When one grasps that formula he discovers that civil servants today who are near the point of retirement and have, say, only one or two years to go will, as the result of the formula provided in this bill, pay in the same amount they are now paying and get, when they retire, a slightly better pension. I could give figures but I will leave that until we get to committee.
That increase in benefit which will be there for civil servants who are going to retire in the next year or two will grow year by year until the tenth year. Those who have precisely ten years to go, when they retire, will get the maximum extra benefits, the marginal benefit that is provided under this formula.
After the tenth year has gone by employees who are still in the service will find that the extra benefit they will get will start to decline. I do not mean just that the extra increment will be less but rather that the total extra benefit that employees will get if they work 11, 12, 20 or 25 years will actually be less than it would be if they were ten-year employees under both plans.
Pensions
When the point is reached where an employee has his full 35 years in he will find that he is just about even. In terms of percentages he will get out of the Canada Pension Plan 25 per cent of his year's maximum pensionable earnings, which at the present time would be $1,250, but in the terms of this bill he will lose 24J per cent of those same earnings. So at the 35-year point there is practically nothing of the extra benefit left, and the retiring civil servant, though he was in two plans, will be getting exactly the same pension within a few cents that he would have got if there had not been the Canada Pension Plan at all.
I just do not think that is good enough. That is why I said a few moments ago that 35 years from now there may well be another Stanley Knowles complaining about the unfair treatment accorded to some of our civil servants because of the nature of this integration formula.
I think that stacking, or decking would have been better. But if we are dealing with a plan where the rates of contribution are higher than in some other plans, a compromise would have been in order. It seems to me that this is not the best kind of compromise that could have been worked out, and I deplore the unevenness of the extra benefits. It starts in the first year and grows up to 10 years and then goes down from 10 years to 35 years.
I also want to urge that when we get into committee on the bill a very clear statement be made on the position of employees who are entitled to retire before they are 65 years of age. There are employees who get their full 35 years of service in at age 60 or 62. Under the Public Service Superannuation Act as it now stands they can retire and draw their full pension. Many persons have come to me about this and I have given them my assurance, an assurance that I am satisfied with, that they will not suffer any loss in their pension under the Public Service Superannuation Act. speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO CORRECT ABUSES AND FOR ORDERLY PAYMENT OF DEBTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope this will be one of those non-controversial bills which fall to the law officers to introduce from time to time. In the unavoidable absence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) the duty to explain it devolves upon me this evening. I know I shall best suit the inclination of the house if I discharge my duty with a few simple words. I can assure the house that at the committee stage the minister will carry the bill.

A complete revision of the Bankruptcy Act being still some time away, this bill is an interim measure amending the Bankruptcy Act to provide remedies to some of the most urgent areas of complaints. The amendments that have been incorporated in the bill may generally be grouped under six different headings:
1.	More adequate means of dealing with frauds connected with bankruptcies will be incorporated in the act and it will also be possible to disseminate information relating to previous bankruptcies so that prospective creditors may better judge the credit rating of their would-be customers.
2.	It will be possible for the court to review transactions which would not come within what may be called moral business practices.
3.	The provisions relating to a proposal made by an insolvent person will be tightened to afford creditors better protection and prevent a proposal from being used as a stalling device to permit a debtor to dissipate his assets.
4.	Bankrupts will be required to deposit with the trustee, for the benefit of their creditors, a certain portion of their salaries, wages or other remuneration.
5.	Certain of the provisions of the act dealing with offences by trustees will be expanded.
6.	A bankrupt corporation will be prevented from applying for a discharge.
The new section 3A of the act will give the Superintendent of Bankruptcy adequate powers to make any inquiry or investigation that may be necessary to expose frauds or other criminal offences relating to estates in bankruptcy that otherwise would not be revealed.
The bill also provides that the trustee will file with the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, in respect of each estate, a report setting out the name of the bankrupt and, where the bankrupt is a corporation, the name and addresses of the directors and officers of the corporation and, when applicable, the names of the persons controlling the day-to-day operations of the bankrupt, as well as the trustee's opinion whether the deficiency between the assets and the liabilities of the bankrupt has or has not been satisfactorily accounted for and, finally, the probable causes of the bankruptcy. The information contained in this report will of course be most valuable to the superintendent in assessing whether the bankrupt's affairs should be investigated by him or not.
June 13, 1966

A separate report setting out only the name of the bankrupt and the names and addresses of the directors and officers of the corporation, where the debtor is a corporation, as well as the names of the persons controlling the day-to-day operations of the bankrupt, will also be required to be filed by the trustee with the official receiver to permit the dissemination of information relating to previous bankruptcies so that prospective creditors may be in a position to better judge the credit rating of their customers.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This bill will incorporate in the Bankruptcy Act the technique used in income tax matters. It will provide that where a person has sold, etc., or purchased, etc., property or services to or from another person with whom the first mentioned person was not dealing at arm's length, and within 12 months of such transaction the first mentioned person becomes bankrupt, the court upon application of the trustee will have the power to review the transaction to inquire whether the consideration was conspicuously excessive or inadequate, and if so give judgment to the trustee for the difference between such consideration and the fair market value of the property or services. These amendments will also provide that where a corporation within 12 months preceding its bankruptcy has redeemed shares or granted a dividend when the corporation was insolvent or that rendered the corporation insolvent, recovery can be had against the directors or against certain of the shareholders of the bankrupt corporation. Other amendments will also be made to other provisions of the act to restrict the rights of creditors that are related to the bankrupt.
Another important amendment will eliminate the possibility of abuses by debtors by giving the creditors, under the direction of the court, more control over the assets of the debtor. These amendments will also provide that if the proposal is not accepted by the creditors or by the court, the debtor will be deemed to have made an assignment on the date the proposal was originally filed with the Official Receiver. Likewise, a proposal that will not be followed through by the debtor will have the same effect as if the debtor had made an assignment in bankruptcy.
Under another amendment the trustee will have to see that the debtor deposits for the benefit of his creditors a certain portion of his salary, wages or other remuneration. It is thought that these provisions will greatly
Bankruptcy Act
help to correct some of the abuses of the bankruptcy process, especially by preventing the obtaining of a too easy discharge from personal debts through bankruptcy proceedings.
The purpose of another amendment is to compel a bankrupt corporation to make a proposal for the benefit of its creditors should the shareholders wish to use a tax loss or stock exchange listing to their own advantage. These amendments will also prevent a corporate shell from being used to obtain further credit to the detriment of new creditors.
Dealing with offences by trustees, the main effect of the amendments in this bill is to make it an offence for a trustee to receive any remuneration or gift other than the remuneration payable out of the estate and to make any kind of arrangement for the splitting of his fees with a solicitor or other person.
I now wish to say just a word or two about the summary administration provisions in the bill. Over a period of years certain abuses have been disclosed in the administration of estates under the Bankruptcy Act and these abuses are attributed in considerable measure to the summary administration provisions. This bill therefore amends the Bankruptcy Act by repealing sections 114 and 115 which contain the summary administration provisions and re-enacting them with certain deletions and changes.
For example, the provision to which I have already referred whereby security is not required under the present act to be deposited by a trustee in respect of each summary administration estate is changed to provide that such security is not required "unless directed by the Official Receiver". The changes made in sections 114 and 115 eliminate or modify a number of the summary administration provisions in order to provide for the stricter administration of the estates to which the summary administration procedure applies.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, a word about the orderly payment of debts. An act of the province of Alberta, called the orderly payment of debts act, was held by the Supreme Court of Canada to be ultra vires the provincial legislatures as impinging upon the federal jurisdiction over bankruptcy and insolvency conferred by section 92(21) of the British North America Act upon the federal parliament. Both Manitoba and Alberta then requested that federal legislation be enacted

June 13, 1966
Bankruptcy Act
of the same character as the provincial legislation. The present bill enacts a new part of the Bankruptcy Act, part X, which closely follows the provincial legislation which was declared ultra vires.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully commend this bill to the house.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-INABILITY TO RECOVER COSTS IN SUPREME COURT ACTION
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-INABILITY TO RECOVER COSTS IN SUPREME COURT ACTION
speechtext:
I rise this evening to bring to the attention of the house an injustice which I consider a constituent of mine, Mr. Charles Ghirardosi, has suffered as a result of having won his case before the Supreme Court of Canada without counsel.
Mr. Ghirardosi's property in Trail, B.C. was expropriated by the British Columbia highways department in 1961. He was told to go to arbitration and the decision of the arbitration was not in his favour. The award which he sought was refused and he had to pay the court costs. He then went to the Supreme Court of British Columbia which set aside the decision in favour of the British Columbia highways department. Nevertheless, again Mr. Ghirardosi had to pay court costs as well as legal expenses to his counsel. Then the minister of highways of British Columbia, Mr. Gaglardi, appealed the decision of the Supreme Court to the Court of Appeal of
June 13. 1966

British Columbia. The Court of Appeal reversed the decision of the Supreme Court of British Columbia and there again my constituent, Mr. Charles Ghirardosi, had to pay the court costs and the expenses of his counsel.
Continuing to seek justice in this case he came to Ottawa with a view to bringing his case before the Supreme Court of Canada. Before leaving Vancouver he asked a solicitor to represent him. The solicitor told him he would not take the case without receiving $12,000 in cash before even starting. Another solicitor offered to undertake this work for $5,000 and still another one demanded $4,000. Finally a solicitor in Ottawa offered to render his services for $850. Mr. Ghirardosi did not have this sort of money so, after thinking it over and reading the Supreme Court act, he decided to appeal his case in person before the Supreme Court of Canada without counsel.
Mr. Ghirardosi is a long-time resident of the Kootenays. He does not have a great deal of formal education but he has a sharp mind. He appealed to the justices of the Supreme Court and obviously convinced them that he had a sound case. The justices gave a judgment which I will read in part as follows:
I would allow the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Court ol Appeal and restore the order of Collins J. The appellant will recover from the respondent his costs in the Court of Appeal and in this court such costs as are taxable in view of the circumstance that he conducted the appeal in person.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the circumstances are that because this man did not have legal counsel all he could possibly obtain was some $100 or so which he paid out for stenographic help and things like that. He is not allowed his costs of coming from Trail to Ottawa, the lost time from his employment, his board and lodging and so on. According to the act, if he had had counsel all these costs would have been allowed. Therefore he considers that he has suffered an injustice in this case.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, he discussed this matter with the member for Kootenay West. Anyone in that constituency who has problems relating to the parliament of Canada and a great many other matters besides discusses them with the member for Kootenay West. I have a wide range of interests. This man also went to see the hon. member for Red Deer and discussed the problem with him. He had heard that the hon. member was interested in this sort of thing, having said in the house on several occasions that he was

On that account, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Red Deer introduced the other day a bill to amend the Canadian Bill of Rights. The purpose of this bill is to provide that there should be no discrimination, by reason of one's belonging to a particular profession or trade or by reason of one's education, in respect of the enjoyment of the basic rights and freedoms recognized by the Canadian Bill of Rights. Finally, the bill provides that each individual shall have the right of access to all courts and tribunals, the right to appear in person before those courts and tribunals and the right to handle his own case. Furthermore, if a decision is rendered in his favour he should be reimbursed his costs, disbursements and reasonable expenses in the same manner as if he were a lawyer handling his own case. This is to emphasize the fact that a private individual should be entitled to obtain full justice in handling his case personally.
I have discussed this matter with Mr. Ghirardosi and other persons, and I have in mind the introduction of a bill to amend the Supreme Court of Canada Act and the rules by adding to section 48 of the act a subsection 2 which would read as follows:
When a party is awarded the costs, he will be entitled to such costs and disbursements with full equality, regardless of whether he has acted in person or through a lawyer.
That may not be worded quite correctly but the intent is there. I have brought this matter to the attention of the house, and I presume that under these circumstances the Solicitor General in the absence of the Minister of Justice, who I know is unavoidably absent this evening, will bring it to the attention of the minister to see whether something can be done to remedy an obvious injustice to a Canadian citizen.

Mr. Speaker, in the overtime period I should like to discuss hockey, particularly professional hockey. I wish to discuss not the players who have played with distinction and brought such distinction to themselves and their sport but the owners of the franchises and the clubs.
Last February 25 I introduced in the house a bill to bring the operation of professional sporting leagues within the purview of the Combines Investigation Act, following the action of the National Hockey league in refusing a franchise to the city of Vancouver for a team to participate in Canada's national game. At that time I said that the amendment I was introducing included all professional sport. However, it is immediately directed at the National Hockey League whose president, Mr. Clarence Campbell, made it clear its owners are interesed only in their own welfare and not in the public interest. This bill would make them recognize their obligations to the public and to Canada whether they wanted to or not.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We must recognize that professional sport in this country and in North America is now very big business. One need only look at the innumerable newspaper clippings on the subject to recognize that. An extract from Maclean's magazine of November 15, 1965, reads:
You can't lick it, you can't join it-it's the sports establishment. It runs sports, sportsmen and (whether they know it or not) the spectators. It's snobbish and arrogant, with rites, rituals and rules -mostly to keep outsiders out. It's a moneyed tyrant with all the appeal of an offside call on a scoring play. So what else is new? The fans actually seem to like it!
Referring to the club owners and the franchise owners it is my considered opinion that there is need for a parliamentary inquiry into the whole operation of professional sporting activities. I have before me a copy of the Congressional Record of the United States where this same subject has come up before various committees of Congress. They have attempted to draft laws to deal with the situation in the United States. I think we in Canada also need a full scale parliamentary inquiry into professional sport in this country.
I welcomed very much the announcement the other day by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that there would be a wide-ranging study into hockey in Canada,


including the relationship between professional and amateur clubs and the impact of hockey on education. I think such an inquiry is extremely important so that the game in Canada can develop in the right way.
It seems to me that an inquiry into hockey is not sufficient for our needs. I earnestly hope that the minister will also consider my bill and the possibility of bringing the operation of the National Hockey League within the purview of the Combines Investigation Act. I think the committee making the inquiry should look into that. I think the committee ought to make a wide-ranging inquiry into the whole operation of professional hockey in Canada.
There is no doubt in my mind that the development of our young athletes and especially the development of amateur hockey players is closely bound up with the operation of the professional leagues. I think many things go on in any professional league that adversely affect hockey in Canada and amateur hockey players.

I think there is a sincere desire on the part of all Canadians involved in hockey both at the official and player level to find answers to some of the important questions facing this great sport.
The subcommittee was established with the following terms of reference: First, to investigate the purposes, structure and functions of the CAHA and other groups as the sports governing bodies for amateur hockey; second,

AGRICULTURE-CHAROLAIS CATTLE-REQUEST FOR PERMISSION TO EXPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: AGRICULTURE-CHAROLAIS CATTLE-REQUEST FOR PERMISSION TO EXPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for drawing this very important matter to my attention and to the attention of the government. First of all I would point out that in my view there is a very considerable difference respecting those cattle which were imported last year, apparently without restriction. No restrictions were made at the time the importations were made and the permits were granted.
Last year was the first year these cattle were ever imported and I think it took a considerable amount of effort on the part of the past minister who introduced this program to effect this importation. In so far as the terms that were granted are concerned, there was no restriction as to what could be done with these cattle with regard to them remaining here or being dealt with as the owner saw fit.

I may point out that other kinds of cattle are imported without restriction as to what may be done by the importer once they are clear of the station. The hon. member has made some valid points and in respect of this year's program I will take them into consideration. I do not think we can or should legislate retroactively. We on this side of the house, like other hon. members, are concerned that we do not interfere with the satisfactory arrangements we have at our border. We now have a very happy situation in that we have in essence established a North American market in respect of our cattle. Other types can be sold in the United States and vice-versa, and we would be very chary about doing anything that would interfere with this situation because I think this kind of market is in the best interests of our cattle producers.
In respect of this year's operation I quite concur that it might be made a condition of the right to bring cattle in that the cattle remain in Canada for as many years as deemed advisable. The members remarks in this regard are worthy of consideration and I assure him that when we are evolving this year's policy we will give consideration and take cognizance of them and the two precedents he brought to my attention with which I was not familiar. I thank him for that information.
